course.title: DevOps and Delivery
course.description: How software is built, packaged, shipped and run reliably: CI/CD, containers, Kubernetes and infrastructure as code.
course.audience: A capable adult who can write and read code and use a terminal, and who wants to understand how changes reach production and stay running. No prior operations experience.

paragraphs: Every change to a running service travels the same path. Someone commits it, a pipeline builds and tests it, it is packaged with everything it needs to run, and it is put in front of users, either all at once or a little at a time. Each part of that path can be done by hand or by machine, and the choices made along it decide how often a team can ship and how often what it ships goes wrong. DevOps and delivery is the engineering of that path, from the commit to the running system and the work of keeping it running.

The research behind the DORA measures found that teams which release small changes often are also the teams whose releases fail least, which runs against the instinct that caution means releasing rarely. Much of the subject follows from asking why that is so, and many of its questions can be settled with arithmetic: how long a pipeline makes a developer wait, how much traffic a new version meets before anyone has checked it, how many copies of a program fit on a machine and how many minutes of downtime an availability target allows. Working those numbers out lets you judge any delivery practice, and any tool that implements one, by what it costs and what it protects against.
outcomes: You'll be able to measure delivery performance and explain why small batches reduce risk.
You'll be able to design a pipeline and choose a rollout strategy for a given risk.
You'll be able to explain what a container is, build an efficient image and read a run command.
You'll be able to describe Kubernetes as a reconciliation system and compute rolling-update and autoscaling numbers.
You'll be able to read declarative infrastructure code, an error budget and the main supply-chain risks.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on How Computers Solve Problems, Linux and the Command Line, Git and Version Control.

modules.title: Delivering change safely
modules.description: Why small, frequent, automated change is safer than rare, large release, and how pipelines and rollout strategies make it so.

modules.title: Containers
modules.description: What a container is, how images are built in layers, and how containers are run and wired together.

modules.title: Kubernetes
modules.description: Declared desired state, the objects that run and expose workloads, and how they scale and take configuration.

modules.title: Infrastructure as code and operation
modules.description: Describing infrastructure in files, reconciling it from Git, observing it, and keeping the supply chain trustworthy.

concepts.title: Lead time for changes
concepts.summary: The time from a commit being made to that commit running in production.

concepts.title: Change failure rate
concepts.summary: The share of deployments to production that cause a failure needing remediation, such as a rollback or hotfix.

concepts.title: Batch size
concepts.summary: The amount of change shipped together; larger batches make failures harder to locate and to undo.

concepts.title: Commit graph
concepts.summary: Git stores history as a graph of commits, each identified by a hash of its content and its parents.

concepts.title: Trunk-based development
concepts.summary: Developers integrate small changes into one shared branch at least daily, keeping other branches short-lived.

concepts.title: Merge conflict
concepts.summary: Two changes edit the same lines, so the tool cannot decide which to keep.

concepts.title: Continuous integration
concepts.summary: Every change is built and tested automatically, on a clean machine, as soon as it is pushed.

concepts.title: Pipeline
concepts.summary: An ordered set of stages, some running in parallel, that a change passes through before release.

concepts.title: Build artifact
concepts.summary: A versioned, immutable output of the build that every later stage and environment reuses unchanged.

concepts.title: Deploy versus release
concepts.summary: Deploying puts code on servers; releasing exposes it to users, and a flag can separate the two.

concepts.title: Canary release
concepts.summary: A new version receives a small share of traffic while its error rate is compared with the old version.

concepts.title: Blue-green deployment
concepts.summary: Two full environments exist; traffic is switched from the live one to the idle one, and back to roll back.

concepts.title: Container
concepts.summary: An ordinary process started with its own view of processes, network and files, and with limits on resources.

concepts.title: Image
concepts.summary: A read-only, layered filesystem and metadata from which containers are started.

concepts.title: Namespaces and cgroups
concepts.summary: Linux features that limit what a process can see (namespaces) and what it can use (cgroups).

concepts.title: Layer cache
concepts.summary: A build step is reused if its instruction and everything before it are unchanged.

concepts.title: Multi-stage build
concepts.summary: A build uses one stage with compilers to produce files, and copies only those files into a small final stage.

concepts.title: Secrets in layers
concepts.summary: Anything written in any layer stays in the image history, even if a later step deletes it.

concepts.title: Published port
concepts.summary: A mapping from a host port to a container port, written host:container.

concepts.title: Volume
concepts.summary: Storage managed outside the container's writable layer, which survives the container.

concepts.title: User-defined network
concepts.summary: A virtual network on which containers reach each other by service name.

concepts.title: Desired state
concepts.summary: The object you submit describes what should exist; controllers act until observed state matches it.

concepts.title: Pod
concepts.summary: The smallest deployable unit: one or more containers sharing a network namespace and storage.

concepts.title: Control plane
concepts.summary: The API server, etcd, scheduler and controller manager, which store and act on cluster state.

concepts.title: Deployment
concepts.summary: An object that manages ReplicaSets so a set of identical pods can be updated gradually.

concepts.title: Label selector
concepts.summary: A query on labels; Services and ReplicaSets use it to find their pods.

concepts.title: Service
concepts.summary: A stable virtual address and name that load-balances to the ready pods matching a selector.

concepts.title: ConfigMap and Secret
concepts.summary: Objects that supply configuration to pods; a Secret is base64-encoded by default, not encrypted.

concepts.title: Requests and limits
concepts.summary: A request is what the scheduler reserves; a limit is the most a container may use.

concepts.title: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler
concepts.summary: Adjusts replica count with desiredReplicas = ceil(currentReplicas x currentMetric / targetMetric).

concepts.title: Declarative description
concepts.summary: Files state what infrastructure should exist; the tool works out the steps.

concepts.title: State
concepts.summary: The tool's record of which real resources correspond to which declarations.

concepts.title: Drift
concepts.summary: A difference between the real infrastructure and its recorded or declared form, usually caused by manual change.

concepts.title: GitOps
concepts.summary: The desired state is stored in Git, and an agent in the cluster pulls and reconciles it continuously.

concepts.title: Metrics, logs and traces
concepts.summary: Numbers over time, discrete events, and the path of one request across services.

concepts.title: Error budget
concepts.summary: The allowed unreliability, equal to 1 minus the SLO, spent by outages and risky changes.

concepts.title: Software supply chain
concepts.summary: Everything that enters a build: source, dependencies, base images, build tools and the pipeline itself.

concepts.title: Digest pinning
concepts.summary: Referring to an image by the SHA-256 of its content, so the reference cannot silently change.

concepts.title: SBOM
concepts.summary: A machine-readable list of the components in a built artifact.

lessons.title: Why shipping is the hard part

lead.text: The table follows one team over a month. The first number, **deployment frequency**, counts how often the team puts a change into production, so a team that made 12 deployments in 4 weeks deploys 12 ÷ 4 = 3 times a week. The second, **lead time for changes**, is the time from a commit being made to that commit running in production, and it starts at the commit, not when someone began writing the code.

The other two measures ask what happened to the changes that were shipped. The **change failure rate** is the share of deployments that needed a rollback or a hotfix, written as a percentage of all deployments, and the **time to restore service** is how long users were affected before the service worked again.

afterFigure.text: These four come from the DORA research programme, which has surveyed thousands of teams since the State of DevOps reports began in 2014. Later DORA material renamed the last measure *failed deployment recovery time* and added a fifth, the deployment rework rate, but the idea is unchanged: one pair says how quickly changes flow, and the other pair says how well they land.

reveal.text: Frequency is a count divided by a period. A rate measured over several weeks smooths out a single quiet or busy week, which is why teams quote it that way.

steps.headline: A commit is made on Monday at 09:00 and reaches production on Wednesday at 15:00. What is its lead time?

workedSteps.text: Lead time starts at the commit, so the clock starts on Monday at 09:00 and stops when the change is running in production.
Monday 09:00 to Wednesday 09:00 is two whole days, and each day has 24 hours.
Wednesday 09:00 to 15:00 is a further 6 hours. Add it to the 48 to get the lead time in hours.
The change spent 54 hours between commit and production, and most of that time is usually waiting rather than work.

steps.headline: In one quarter a team made 48 deployments, and 6 of them needed a rollback or a hotfix. What is its change failure rate?

workedSteps.text: The rate compares failed deployments with all deployments, not with the successful ones.
Divide 6 by 48 to get a fraction of one, then multiply by 100 to express it as a percentage.
Convert the fraction to a percentage. Give the change failure rate.

reveal.text: Every one of the forty is a suspect, and they interact, so the search can be longer than forty separate checks. The next screen compares this with shipping the changes one at a time.

lead.text: The amount of change that ships together is called the **batch size**. In the figure the same forty changes are shipped in two ways. As one release they form a batch of 40, so when checkout fails the cause could be any change in it, and two changes together may fail where neither does alone.
Shipped as forty releases of one change each, the failure appears right after one specific release, and the cause is the single change inside it.

afterFigure.text: The same logic makes recovery cheaper. Undoing one small change is a small, well-understood action, whereas undoing a batch of forty either throws away thirty-nine good changes or means untangling them under pressure. *Smaller batches therefore reduce both the time to find a failure and the cost of reversing it*, which is why frequent deployment tends to go with a low change failure rate and not against it.

lead.text: A team could raise its deployment frequency by deploying carelessly, and the change failure rate would expose that at once. A team could lower its failure rate by deploying almost never, and its frequency and lead time would expose that. Because each speed measure is read beside a stability measure, neither can be improved by quietly sacrificing the other.

DORA's findings across many organisations are that the best teams score well on both pairs together, so speed and stability are not a trade. This is the reason the course treats delivery as something to be engineered: the practices in the following lessons exist to make small, frequent changes safe.

afterFigure.text: The word *DevOps* names the working arrangement that makes this possible. It is not a job title or a set of tools: the people who write a change share responsibility for how it runs, so they feel a failure directly and have a reason to make the next change smaller.

reveal.text: It is read together with the speed measures: a rate of 15 per cent is easier to judge beside a deployment frequency and a lead time than alone.
Smaller batches mean fewer candidates per failure and an easier undo, so the usual result is a lower or equal failure rate and much faster diagnosis, even though the team now deploys more often.

blocks.text: A team's records for one month might show 12 production deployments in 4 weeks, and a change committed on a Monday at 09:00 that was running in production by the Wednesday at 15:00. Figures like these say how quickly a team ships and how well its releases land, and the research programme known as DORA has used the same few measures to compare thousands of teams since the State of DevOps reports began in 2014.

What the measures expose is the real difficulty of shipping software, which is that every change carries some risk of breaking what already works. When a release does break something, someone has to find the change responsible and undo it, and how long that takes depends on how much the release contained. Once you can work the measures out from a team's own records, you can tell whether its way of working is making those failures rarer and quicker to recover from.

recap.keyIdea: Delivery performance is four numbers, two for speed and two for stability, and shipping smaller batches improves both.

blocks.text: Deployment frequency and lead time describe how quickly changes reach production, and change failure rate and time to restore service describe how well they land. Because the pairs are read together, a team cannot look good by sacrificing one for the other.
Batch size is the reason small, frequent releases are safer: a failure in a release of one change has one suspect and one thing to undo, while a failure in a release of forty has forty.

lessons.title: Version control for continuous change

reveal.text: No commit is made. The command adds a label, and the commit graph is unchanged until you commit something while on fix.

lead.text: Git stores history as a **commit graph**. Each commit records a snapshot of the project and the identity of its parent, which is the commit it was built on, and a short hash such as `d40` names the commit. The first figure shows four commits in a row, each pointing back to its parent.

A **branch** is a name attached to one commit, so `main` in the figure is only a label sitting on the newest commit. Running `git switch -c fix` adds a second label at the same commit and creates no commit and copies no file, which is why a branch is created in an instant however large the project is.

afterFigure.text: The label moves only when you commit. In the third view a new commit `b58` has been made while `fix` was checked out, so `fix` has moved to it and `main` has stayed where it was. The two lines of work have now *diverged*, and everything that follows in this lesson depends on how far they drift apart before they are joined again.

diagram.alt: A commit graph of four commits with hash labels and the main pointer on the newest. Switching to a new branch adds a second pointer to the same commit, and committing moves only that pointer to a new commit.

lead.text: While you work on a branch, the rest of the team keeps merging into `main`. Suppose 5 developers each merge 2 commits a day. After one working day `main` has gained 5 × 2 × 1 = 10 commits that your branch has never seen, and after twenty days it has gained 5 × 2 × 20 = 200.

The two bars are drawn to the same scale, so the long branch is twenty times as far behind as the short one. Isolation feels safe because nothing disturbs your work, but the isolation is paid for later: *every commit you have not seen is a change your code might disagree with*.

afterFigure.text: Nothing is saved by waiting, because the amount to reconcile only grows. A short branch is merged while the others' changes are few and fresh in everyone's mind, and the work of joining is small. This is the same argument as batch size in the previous lesson, applied to the length of time a change stays unintegrated.

lead.text: When Git joins two branches it combines the changes each made since they parted. If one branch changed a line and the other changed different lines, the merge is automatic. If both changed the *same* lines, Git cannot decide which version to keep, stops, and reports a **merge conflict** for a person to resolve.

A conflict is therefore not a sign that someone did something wrong. It is what happens when two people work on the same place without seeing each other's work, and the longer the branches have been apart, the more places there are for that to happen and the less either author remembers about their change.

afterFigure.text: Seen this way, a conflict is a symptom of *delayed integration*. Resolving fewer, smaller ones is better than dreading many large ones, and the remedy is to merge sooner, not to take more care while resolving.

lead.text: In **trunk-based development** every developer merges small changes into one shared branch, the trunk, at least once a day, and any other branch lives for hours or a day or two. The DORA research found this practice associated with better delivery performance, and the reasoning is the arithmetic above: a branch that never gets more than a day behind never faces more than a day's worth of other people's work.

The obvious objection is that a large feature cannot be finished in a day. The answer is a **feature flag**, a condition in the code that keeps a new feature switched off until it is ready. The unfinished code is merged and shipped in small pieces, but no user reaches it, so integration is separated from release.

afterFigure.text: Merging is also gated by a **pull request**, a proposal to merge a branch that colleagues review and that automated checks run against. Reviews work best on small diffs, because a reviewer can understand a change of a few dozen lines and cannot meaningfully read a thousand. Small batches help here as well.

reveal.text: A flag keeps the code in the trunk and out of users' hands, so each day's piece is integrated while the feature as a whole is still off.
24 commits is a manageable amount to read through, while the earlier 180 was not, and the rule costs nothing except the habit of merging in smaller pieces.

lessons.orientation: Read a commit graph, and choose a branching approach that keeps integration frequent.
lessons.nextAction: Build a pipeline that tests every merge automatically and compute how long it takes.

blocks.text: In a project with a million lines of code, `git switch -c fix` creates a branch called `fix` in a fraction of a second, however long the project's history. A command that fast cannot be copying the project, and seeing what it does instead explains both how Git keeps two lines of work apart and why joining them back together is where the cost of a branch lies.

That cost grows the longer a branch lives. If a feature branch lasts twenty working days while five colleagues each merge two commits a day, then 200 commits will have landed on the shared line before it returns, and each of them is a chance for the two lines of work to disagree. Working out that number for a team tells you how far a branch falls behind, and why teams that merge into one shared line every day meet far fewer merge conflicts than teams whose branches live for weeks.

intro.promise: By the end you'll read a commit graph, work out how far a branch falls behind, and say why merge conflicts are a symptom of delayed integration.
intro.whyItMatters: Branching practice sets how large each integration is, which is the batch size of the previous lesson.

recap.keyIdea: A branch is only a pointer, and the cost of keeping it apart grows with every commit that lands elsewhere, so integrate small and often.

blocks.text: Creating a branch copies nothing, but each day it stays apart the shared line gains more commits it has not seen, and merge conflicts are what that distance feels like. Trunk-based development keeps the distance short by merging at least daily, hiding unfinished work behind feature flags and reviewing small pull requests.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson makes every merge to the trunk run automatic checks, so that a short branch is also a safe one.

lessons.title: Continuous integration and the pipeline

reveal.text: Stages that run one after another simply add, to 30 minutes, so the author of a failing commit may wait up to half an hour to hear about it.

lead.text: **Continuous integration** means that every change pushed to the shared branch is built and tested automatically on a clean machine, not on the author's laptop where an unrecorded setting may hide a fault. The ordered set of checks it runs is a **pipeline**, and each step in it is a stage.

The first figure compares two arrangements of the same five stages. In the first the stages run one after another, so the times add to 30 minutes. A failure in unit tests then arrives after 2 + 5 + 8 = 15 minutes, by which time the author has started something else and must stop and return to a change they had stopped thinking about.

afterFigure.text: The second view reaches the same checks in 20 minutes. It builds once, runs lint, unit tests and integration tests side by side because none needs another's result, and deploys only when all three have passed. Nothing has been dropped, and the time has fallen because stages that do not depend on each other no longer wait.

reveal.text: The three parallel stages finish when the slowest does, so the 11-minute unit tests set the time, and the lint and integration tests finish inside them.

lead.text: The time a person waits is the **wall-clock time**, and for stages that overlap it is set by the slowest of them, not by their sum. A pipeline's total is the sum of the stages that must run in sequence, with each group of parallel stages counted once at the length of its longest member.

A single slow stage can be shortened by **sharding**, which splits its work into parts that run at once. A 36-minute test suite divided into 3 equal shards takes 36 ÷ 3 = 12 minutes, provided the parts are balanced, because the stage ends only when the last shard ends.

afterFigure.text: Balance matters. If one shard receives 16 minutes of work and the others 10, the stage takes 16 minutes and not 12, so the gain depends on splitting the tests evenly. Set-up time for each shard also counts, which is why sharding stops paying once the parts become very small.

The suite that took 32 minutes in one piece now delays the pipeline by 8.

workedSteps.text: The build must finish first, because the three checks use its output.
The three checks overlap, so count only the longest, which is the integration tests.
Deploy waits for the checks, so add its 2 minutes. Give the total pipeline time.

lead.text: The output of the build stage is a **build artifact**: a package or image with a version, which is never altered after it is made. If every environment rebuilt the code, the version tested in staging and the version running in production would be separate builds made at different times, and a difference between them (a newer dependency, say) could cause a failure no test saw.

In the second view the code is built once and the same artifact v1.4 moves to test, staging and production. Each environment receives what the previous one tested, byte for byte, and what differs between environments is configuration supplied from outside, a point the twelve-factor method makes and the containers module returns to.

afterFigure.text: A pipeline is itself written down as a file kept in the repository, so that it is reviewed and versioned like the code it builds. Current tools such as GitHub Actions and GitLab CI read a configuration file from the repository for exactly this reason.

lead.text: Stages are ordered by how cheaply they catch failures. Lint and unit tests take seconds or minutes and catch most mistakes, so they run first and stop the pipeline early, while integration tests and deployment take longer and cost more, so they run once the cheap checks have passed. Putting the slowest test first would make every failure wait for it.

A passing pipeline is limited by what it checks. If no test covers a path, the pipeline reports green for a bug on it, so *green means that the checks that exist passed*, and the number of useful checks decides how far that can be trusted.

afterFigure.text: A pipeline that is red most of the time is just as useless, because people begin to ignore it. The practice that goes with it is to treat a red trunk as the team's first job, so that the shared line is almost always releasable.

reveal.text: The stage ends with its last shard, so 14 minutes is what the pipeline waits for. Rebalancing to 8 minutes each would save a further 6.

blocks.text: A one-line fix pushed to a shared repository can wait twenty-eight minutes before a failing unit test reports that it is wrong, and by then its author has usually moved on to something else. The failure then costs the effort of remembering what the change was as well as the effort of correcting it, while the same report in the first minute would have been dealt with before the author's attention left the change.

The automated checks that run on every pushed change are arranged into a pipeline, and how soon it reports depends as much on how its stages are arranged as on how fast each one is. Which checks run first, which can run side by side and how a slow test suite is split across machines all have arithmetic answers, and working them out lets you shorten the wait for feedback without dropping any of the checks.

blocks.text: Wall-clock time is the sum of the stages that wait for each other, with each parallel group counted at its slowest member, and sharding shortens a long stage when the parts are balanced. Because the same artifact is promoted through every environment, a green result in staging is a statement about what will run in production.

lessons.title: Releasing without fear

lead.text: **Deploying** a version means putting it on the servers, and **releasing** it means letting users reach it. The two can be done at different moments, and the strategies in the figure differ in how they handle the gap between them.

A **rolling update** replaces instances a batch at a time: with 10 instances replaced 2 at a time the update takes 10 ÷ 2 = 5 batches, and for a while both versions serve users. **Blue-green deployment** keeps two full environments, the live one (blue) and an idle one (green) that holds the new version, and releases by switching all traffic to green, so rolling back is a switch back. A **canary release** sends a small share of traffic to the new version and compares its errors with the old one before widening the share.

afterFigure.text: Each strategy has a price. Blue-green needs capacity for two production environments at the moment of the switch, which a rolling update does not, and a canary needs someone, or something, watching the right measure, because a canary that nobody reads protects nobody.

reveal.text: With one batch at a time, only 3 of 18 instances are out of service at once, so 15 of them keep serving users throughout.

lead.text: Suppose a service receives 2,000 requests a second and the canary is given 5 per cent. The canary then handles 2,000 × 0.05 = 100 requests a second, and the remaining 1,900 go to the old version. If the canary fails on 2 per cent of its requests, that is 100 × 0.02 = 2 errors a second.

Two errors a second sounds small, and the useful comparison is the *rate*. If the old version also fails on about 2 per cent, the new one is no worse, and the rollout can widen to 25 per cent, then 50, then 100. If the old version fails on 0.1 per cent, the canary is twenty times worse and should be stopped, even though the total number of errors is still low, because only a small share of users has met it.

afterFigure.text: This is why a canary reduces the change failure rate from lesson one: a bad version harms 5 per cent of users for a few minutes instead of all of them, and the time to restore service is the time to send that 5 per cent back.

reveal.text: Code can be redeployed but data cannot be reinstated by a redeploy, so an irreversible schema change turns a safe rollback into a recovery from backup.

lead.text: Redeploying old code undoes the code. It does not undo changes to a database, so a migration that drops or renames a column cannot be reversed by a rollback, and 'we can always roll back' is true only of the code.

The safe pattern is **expand, then contract**. First *expand*: add the new column and leave the old one, so old and new code both work. Then *migrate*: write to both columns and copy the old rows across. Only when no old version can run anywhere do you *contract* and drop the old column. In the figure, a rollback is safe in the first two views and unsafe in the third.

afterFigure.text: The same staging lets a rolling update or a canary work at all. During those strategies old and new versions run at once, so the database has to suit both.

reveal.text: It was met in the trunk lesson as the way unfinished work is merged daily; here it is the way a deploy and a release are pulled apart.

lead.text: With a **feature flag** the new code is deployed switched off and released later, to staff first, then to 1 per cent of users, then to everyone. If something fails, turning the flag off restores the old behaviour in seconds with no deployment, which makes it the fastest rollback of the three.

A flag has a cost. Each one adds a branch to the code and a state to test, and a flag that stays after its feature is fully released leaves dead paths behind, so a flag is removed once the release is complete. Teams track the flags they have and delete them, just as they delete merged branches.

afterFigure.text: Together the strategies serve the two measures from lesson one: canaries and flags lower the change failure rate by limiting who sees a bad change, and the ability to switch off or switch back lowers the time to restore service.

reveal.text: That doubling is the price of an instant switch and an instant rollback, and it applies for as long as the old environment is kept ready.

blocks.text: A deployment that goes wrong at 2,000 requests a second affects 2,000 requests a second. The same version, sent to 5 per cent of the traffic first, affects 100, and if its errors show up in those 100 the team can stop before anyone else has met the fault. Between these two outcomes there is no difference in the code, only in the way it was exposed.

Releasing a version is a separate act from deploying it, and a release strategy makes that act smaller, slower and reversible. Each one trades something for its safety, either spare capacity, a longer rollout or a flag left in the code, and choosing between them is a matter of the risk of the change.

blocks.text: A rolling update replaces instances in batches, blue-green switches whole environments at the price of double capacity, and a canary sends a small share of traffic and compares its error rate with the old version. A rollback undoes code but not data, so schema changes go through expand, migrate and contract, and flags give the fastest switch-off at the cost of cleaning them up.

lessons.title: What a container is

lead.text: Software that runs on one machine often fails on another because the libraries, the tool versions and the settings differ. A **container** removes the difference by starting a program together with its own files, so that it sees the same files wherever it runs. It does this without creating a new computer: the program is still an ordinary process on the host, as the first view of the figure shows, where the host's process list includes the container's `nginx` and `postgres`.

Two features of the Linux kernel do the work. **Namespaces** limit what a process can *see*, so that the container gets its own process numbers, network, hostname and filesystem, and the second view shows `nginx` seeing itself as process 1 and nothing else. **Control groups**, or cgroups, limit what it can *use*, such as memory and processor time.

afterFigure.text: A container limited to 512 MiB of memory that tries to use 600 MiB is stopped by the kernel for exceeding its limit, and the other containers on the host are unaffected. The container is therefore not a special object that Linux added, but a way of combining features it already had.

reveal.text: A limit is enforced by the kernel itself, which is how a container that exceeds its memory is stopped without the host being harmed.
They share the host kernel. This is what makes them quick to start and also what separates them from a virtual machine.

lead.text: A **virtual machine** is a complete computer in software. A hypervisor presents virtual hardware, and each machine boots its own operating system with its own kernel, so the stack in the first view repeats a guest operating system for every machine. That gives strong separation at the cost of gigabytes of disk and seconds or minutes to start.

A container starts a process on the kernel that is already running, so there is no operating system to boot and it can be ready in milliseconds. The second view shows the cost of the saving. Because every container shares the host kernel, a flaw in that kernel is a flaw under all of them, and a container can run only programs built for the host's kernel.

afterFigure.text: For that reason a container is often described as lighter than a virtual machine, which is correct about weight but misleading about nature: it is isolation by rules inside one kernel, not by a separate machine.

lead.text: An **image** is a read-only package of layered files and the metadata needed to run them, such as which program to start. It is not running anything, and it can be stored, copied and shared. Starting a container from an image adds a thin writable layer on top, in which the container's own changes are kept, and the image layers beneath stay untouched.

Because the image layers are never changed, any number of containers can start from the same image. The third figure shows three containers from one 200 MB image, each with a writable layer of about 5 MB, so the disk holds 200 + 3 × 5 = 215 MB, not 600.

afterFigure.text: Stopping or deleting a container deletes its writable layer and nothing else, so the image is still there to start another. Images are kept in a **registry**, a server that stores them under names and versions, from which a host pulls an image before it can run it.

blocks.text: Run ps on a Linux host that is running a container and the program inside it appears in the list, numbered like any other process. Inside the container the same program believes it is the first and only process on the machine, with its own network and its own filesystem. Both descriptions are true, and the difference between them is the whole of what a container is.

A container is not a small computer. It is a process that the kernel has been asked to isolate and to limit, and understanding that removes most of the mystery about why containers start so quickly, why they are so easy to copy and where their isolation stops.

intro.promise: By the end you'll explain a container as a process with limits on a shared kernel, contrast it with a virtual machine, and tell an image from a container.
intro.whyItMatters: Every later lesson on Kubernetes and pipelines assumes this picture.

recap.keyIdea: A container is an isolated, limited process on the host's kernel, started from an image that is shared and never changed.

blocks.text: Namespaces control what a containerised process can see and cgroups control what it can use, which together make an ordinary process behave as though it had a machine to itself. It shares the host kernel, unlike a virtual machine, and it starts from an image whose read-only layers many containers can share, each adding only a thin writable layer.

lessons.title: Building images well

reveal.text: Two are rebuilt, COPY src ./src and the CMD after it. The next screen explains the rule that decides this and shows the same Dockerfile beside a worse ordering.

lead.text: Building an image runs a Dockerfile one instruction at a time, and each instruction that changes the filesystem produces a **layer**. The builder keeps these layers, and it reuses a layer from the **layer cache** when the instruction is identical and every layer before it was reused as well. As soon as one layer has to be rebuilt, all the layers after it are rebuilt too.

In the first view, only `src/app.js` has changed. The base image, the copy of `package.json` and the dependency install are unchanged, so they come from the cache, and only the copy of the source and the final `CMD` are rebuilt, which is 2 of the 5 steps. The slow `npm ci` was skipped because its inputs, the package file, are the same as last time.

afterFigure.text: The second view does the same job in a worse order. COPY . . brings the whole project in before the install, so any edited file changes that layer and invalidates everything after it, including npm ci. The rule that follows is to put what changes rarely, such as the dependency list, early, and what changes constantly, such as the source, late.

reveal.text: Each of them after the first changes or follows a changed layer, so the dependency install is repeated on every edit, which is the cost of copying everything first.

lead.text: Building software often needs tools that running it does not, such as compilers and package caches. If they stay in the shipped image it grows, and every extra program is something that could contain a vulnerability. A **multi-stage build** uses several `FROM` lines: the first stage has the tools and produces files, and a later stage starts from a small base and copies in only those files.

The stages are named with the keyword `AS`, as in `FROM golang AS build`, and a later stage takes files from it with `COPY --from=build`. In the figure the build stage is 1,200 MB and the final stage is 180 MB, drawn to the same scale, so what ships is 1,200 − 180 = 1,020 MB smaller.

afterFigure.text: The smaller image also pulls faster and has less in it to attack, which is why most production images are built in stages.

lead.text: Layers are never edited after they are made. If one step copies a .env file into the image and a later step runs rm on it, the later layer records that the file is hidden, but the earlier layer still holds its contents, and anyone who pulls the image can extract them. Secrets therefore never belong in the build, and are supplied when the container runs or through the build tool's secret mount.

Naming the base image has a similar trap. A tag such as `node:22` or `latest` is a label that its owner can move to a new image, so two builds of the same Dockerfile on different days may start from different bases. A **digest**, the sha256 hash of the image's content, names one image exactly, so pinning a base by digest makes the build repeatable.

afterFigure.text: The tag in an example such as node:22 is only an example. Pick the version your project supports, and pin it more tightly than a tag when repeatability matters.

blocks.text: Two Dockerfiles can build exactly the same image, and yet after a one-line edit to the source one of them takes four minutes to rebuild while the other takes four seconds. Nothing differs between them except the order of their instructions, because the builder keeps the result of each instruction and reuses it on the next build whenever it can.

Reading a Dockerfile with that in mind, as a stack of saved results as well as a recipe, lets you predict how much of a rebuild will be repeated before you start it, and rewrite the file so that the slow steps are rarely run again. The same reading shows how to leave the build tools out of the finished image, and why a secret should never pass through a build at all.

recap.keyIdea: Order instructions so that what changes least comes first, ship only a small final stage and never put a secret in a layer.

blocks.text: A layer is reused when its instruction and everything before it are unchanged, so copying dependency files and installing them before the source keeps the slow step cached. A multi-stage build ships only the final stage, and because layers only ever add, a secret deleted in a later step remains in the image history.

lessons.title: Running and connecting containers

reveal.text: Port 8080, because the host port is written first. The next screen shows how the two numbers relate.

lead.text: A container has its own network, so a program listening on port 80 inside it is not reachable from the host by default. **Publishing a port** makes a mapping between a port on the host and a port in the container, written with the flag `-p` as *host:container*. With `-p 8080:80`, traffic that arrives at the host's port 8080 is passed to port 80 in the container.

The figure shows two mappings of the same server. In the first the browser uses localhost:8080 and in the second localhost:3000, while nginx listens on port 80 in both. The number inside the container is fixed by the program, and the number on the host is your choice, so two containers that both listen on 80 can run side by side as long as they are published on different host ports.

afterFigure.text: A common slip is to read the pair backwards. The host side is the one you type into the browser, and it is always first.

diagram.alt: A browser reaches a container through a published port. With -p 8080:80 the browser uses host port 8080 and the container's nginx listens on port 80. With -p 3000:80 the browser uses host port 3000 and the container still listens on 80.

lead.text: A container's writable layer lives only as long as the container does. A database running with no volume keeps its rows in that layer, and when the container is removed the rows go with it, so recreating the container from the same image gives an empty database.

A **volume** is storage that Docker manages outside the container, and it is attached at a path such as `/var/lib/db` with the flag `-v`. The container writes to that path as usual, but the data lands in the volume, which survives the container's removal and can be attached to the next container started.

afterFigure.text: This is why containers are treated as disposable. A misbehaving container is replaced from its image and not repaired by logging in and editing it, and anything that must be kept lives in a volume or a service outside the container.

steps.headline: Read this command: docker run -d -p 5432:5432 -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres.

workedSteps.text: The flag `-d` runs the container in the background, and the last word names the image, `postgres`.
The flag `-p` publishes port 5432 on the host to port 5432 in the container, host side first.
The flag `-v` attaches the volume to the directory where the database writes. Give the name of the volume.
The data in that directory survives removal of the container, because it is stored in the volume.

steps.headline: Read this command: docker run -p 8000:5000 -v uploads:/app/files web.

workedSteps.text: The last word, `web`, is the image to run, and `-v` keeps the files in `/app/files` in a volume called `uploads`.
The program inside listens on port 5000, which is the second number of the `-p` pair.
The first number is the host's port. Give the host port a browser would use.

reveal.text: It uses the service name, db. The next screen explains why that works without anyone looking up an address.

lead.text: A **user-defined network** is a private virtual network that containers join. On it each container can be reached by its service name, so a web program can connect to the host name `db`, and Docker resolves it to the database container's current address. The addresses change every time a container is recreated, which is why names are used and not numbers.

The compose file in the figure puts web and db on one network and publishes only one port, 8080 on the host to 3000 in web. The database has no published port, so nothing outside the network can reach it, and web can. Publishing as little as possible is the cheapest safeguard there is.

afterFigure.text: Settings such as the database host are passed in as environment variables, as in DATABASE_HOST: db, and are not written into the image. The twelve-factor approach asks for exactly this, so the same image runs unchanged in development and in production, with only its configuration differing.

blocks.text: The command docker run nginx starts a web server that listens on port 80, yet a browser pointed at the same machine finds nothing there. The server is running inside the container's own network, which nothing outside the container can see, and the program has no means of changing that from the inside.

Everything about how a container meets the world is set by the flags of its run command, which say which of its ports can be reached from the host, which of its data outlives it and which other containers it can talk to. Reading those flags correctly lets you say, before anything runs, where a service will answer and what a restart will lose.

intro.promise: By the end you'll read a docker run command, say which data survives a container and which containers can reach each other.
intro.whyItMatters: Every Kubernetes object in the next lessons is a larger version of these ideas.

recap.keyIdea: A container's ports are private until published, its data lasts only if it is on a volume, and containers on one network reach each other by name.

blocks.text: The flag `-p` publishes a host port to a container port with the host first, and `-v` attaches a volume so that data outlives the container. Containers on one user-defined network find each other by service name, and settings arrive as environment variables, which is what lets a container be thrown away and replaced.

lessons.title: Desired state and the control loop

reveal.text: It will create 2. The next screen explains the loop that arrives at that number.

lead.text: With a plain container runtime you give commands: start this, stop that. With Kubernetes you submit a description, called a manifest, of what should exist, such as 'three copies of this container', and that is the **desired state**. The cluster then does whatever is needed to make the world match it.

The work is done by controllers running a loop: they **observe** what is running, **compare** it with the desired state and **act** on the difference, then repeat. In the figure, with 5 replicas wanted and 3 running, the controller creates 5 − 3 = 2 pods, and with 3 wanted and 4 running it deletes 1. With 3 and 3 it does nothing, and it keeps watching.

afterFigure.text: This is called **reconciliation**, and it explains the behaviour that gives Kubernetes its reputation for self-healing. If a pod dies, the observed state falls below the desired one, and the next pass of the loop creates a replacement. Nobody had to notice.

reveal.text: The loop acts in both directions: too few and it creates, too many and it removes the surplus.

lead.text: Kubernetes does not run containers one by one. The unit it creates, schedules and deletes is the **pod**, which holds one container in the usual case and several in the case of tightly coupled helpers. The containers in a pod share one IP address and can reach each other on `localhost`, and they share any storage the pod defines.

A pod is not repaired. If it dies, a controller creates a replacement, which is a new pod with a new IP address and not the old one restarted in place. Anything that must reach it therefore cannot rely on the address, a problem the next lesson solves.

afterFigure.text: So a pod with two containers still has a single IP address, and that is the reason a web container and a log-shipping helper can talk over localhost without any network setup.

lead.text: The **control plane** holds the cluster's brain. The *API server* is the front door that every request passes through, and *etcd* is the database that stores all cluster state. The *scheduler* chooses a node for each new pod, and the *controller manager* runs the controllers whose loops were described above.

The **nodes** do the work. On each node a *kubelet* receives the list of pods assigned to it and makes sure their containers are running, by asking a *container runtime* to start them, and *kube-proxy* handles the networking rules for Services, the stable addresses in front of pods that the next lesson introduces. This answers a common misunderstanding: Kubernetes does not run your containers itself, it asks a kubelet, which asks a runtime.

afterFigure.text: All of the components talk through the API server, and none of them keeps its own copy of the truth. That is what makes the loop reliable, because every observation and every declared state is read from one place.

reveal.text: Only the API server talks to it directly, so the rest of the cluster reads and writes state through the API server.

lead.text: Suppose you run kubectl apply with a manifest that asks for 3 replicas. The command sends the manifest to the API server, which checks it and accepts it. The API server writes the desired state into etcd, so it is now recorded as the cluster's intention.

The controllers notice the gap between 3 desired and 0 running and create three pods. The scheduler picks a node for each one, and the kubelet on that node sees a pod assigned to it and asks the runtime to start its containers. The figure steps through the four moments.

afterFigure.text: Every step is a separate component reading or writing the stored state, and none calls the next directly, so any one of them can fail and restart without losing the request.

blocks.text: A Kubernetes manifest for a web application can contain the line replicas: 3, which states that three copies of the program should be running at all times. Nothing in the file says how to start them or what to do if one fails, because the cluster is left to make the world match the statement and to keep it matching for as long as the statement stands.

The part that does this work is a control loop, and Kubernetes is built from such loops throughout. Once you see how a loop compares what is declared with what exists, you can work out what the cluster will create or delete in a given situation, and place each component of the control plane and of a node by the part it plays in that loop.

intro.promise: By the end you'll compute what a controller creates or deletes to reach a declared state, name the control plane and node components, and trace a kubectl apply.
intro.whyItMatters: Every object in the rest of the module is declared state with a controller behind it.

recap.keyIdea: Kubernetes keeps a declared state true with control loops that observe, compare and act, and a pod that dies is replaced, not repaired.

blocks.text: You declare what should exist, and controllers compare it with what is running and create or delete pods to remove the difference. The control plane stores and decides through the API server, etcd, the scheduler and the controller manager, while each node's kubelet asks a container runtime to run the pods it has been given.

lessons.title: Deployments, labels and Services

reveal.text: Two receive it. The selector chooses by label and only ready pods are used, as the next screen shows.

lead.text: Pods come and go, and each replacement has a new IP address, so nothing can depend on a pod's address. A **Service** supplies a stable virtual address and name in front of a changing set of pods, and it finds those pods by their labels. A **label** is a key and value attached to an object, such as `app=web`, and a **selector** is a query on labels, such as 'every pod with `app=web`'.

In the figure the Service with selector `app=web` sends traffic to the two pods that carry that label and are ready. The pod labelled `app=db` does not match, and the `app=web` pod that is not yet ready is skipped until it passes its **readiness** check, so a starting pod is never sent requests it cannot answer.

afterFigure.text: Labels are only labels. In the second view one pod's label is edited to `app=debug` and it falls out of the Service at once, which is a useful way to take a pod out of rotation for inspection without deleting it. Services come in types: `ClusterIP`, the default, is reachable only inside the cluster, `NodePort` opens a port on every node and `LoadBalancer` asks the cloud for an external address.

lead.text: Users do not usually create pods by hand. A **Deployment** declares the pod template and the number of replicas, and it manages a **ReplicaSet**, the object whose controller keeps that number of identical pods running. When you change the image, the Deployment creates a second ReplicaSet for the new version and moves pods from the old one to the new one gradually.

The figure shows this for three replicas. Before the update, the first ReplicaSet holds all three pods. During it, the second ReplicaSet has two new pods and the first has two old ones, so four pods exist, and by the end the first holds none. The old ReplicaSet is kept with zero pods, so a rollback is a move in the opposite direction.

afterFigure.text: Because the Service selects by label and ready state, traffic follows the move without anyone changing the Service. A new pod joins when it is ready and an old pod leaves when it is removed.

lead.text: The speed and safety of the move are set by two values. **maxSurge** is how many pods *above* the desired number may exist during the update, and **maxUnavailable** is how many pods *below* it may be unavailable. Each can be a count or a percentage of the desired replicas, and the defaults are 25 per cent for both.

A percentage rarely gives a whole number, so Kubernetes rounds it, and it rounds in the safe direction. The surge rounds *up*, which gives a little more capacity, and the unavailable count rounds *down*, which allows a little less loss. For 10 replicas and 25 per cent each, the surge is 2.5, rounded up to 3, and the unavailable count is 2.5, rounded down to 2, so at most 10 + 3 = 13 pods exist and at least 10 − 2 = 8 are available.

afterFigure.text: Setting `maxSurge` to 1 and `maxUnavailable` to 0 gives the most cautious update. With 3 replicas, at most 4 pods exist and all 3 stay available, because a new pod must be ready before an old one is taken away.

lessons.orientation: Use labels and selectors to connect a Service to its pods, and compute the pod counts of a rolling update.
lessons.nextAction: Keep configuration out of images, set requests and limits, and compute what the autoscaler will do.

blocks.text: A pod that crashes is replaced by a new pod, and the new pod has a different IP address. Anything that held the old address now points at nothing, and in a cluster where pods are replaced all day long, that happens constantly. A program cannot depend on a pod's address, so it needs something steadier to depend on.

Kubernetes provides that steadier thing as a Service, which picks out its pods by the labels attached to them, so a replacement pod is found as soon as it carries the right label and is ready. The same labels let a Deployment replace one version of an application with the next without a moment of downtime, and two of its settings fix how many pods may exist during the replacement, so you can work out in advance how much spare capacity an update needs and how much of the application may be missing while it runs.

intro.promise: By the end you'll say which pods a Service sends traffic to, and compute the greatest and smallest pod counts of a rolling update, including the rounding.
intro.whyItMatters: This is the working core of running an application on Kubernetes.

recap.keyIdea: A Service reaches the ready pods that match its label selector, and a Deployment replaces pods within limits set by `maxSurge` and `maxUnavailable`.

blocks.text: Labels and selectors let a Service follow a changing set of pods, using only those that are ready. A Deployment moves replicas from an old ReplicaSet to a new one, and its limits are the desired count plus the surge, rounded up, at most, and the desired count minus the unavailable number, rounded down, at least.

lessons.title: Configuration, resources and scaling

lead.text: The twelve-factor approach asks that configuration, which varies between environments, be kept apart from the code. In Kubernetes a **ConfigMap** holds ordinary settings such as a hostname or a feature setting, and a **Secret** holds sensitive values such as a password. Both are supplied to a pod as environment variables or as files, so the same image runs in development and in production with different settings.

The name Secret suggests more than it provides. By default its values are only base64-encoded, an encoding that anyone can reverse. In the figure the stored text `cGFzc3dvcmQ=` decodes to the word `password`, with no key involved. What protects a Secret is access control over who may read it, and encryption at rest if the cluster has been set up for it.

afterFigure.text: Putting configuration in the cluster has another benefit: changing a setting does not require building a new image, and a build in a pipeline can stay identical from test to production, as lesson three argued.

Sixteen fit. The next screen explains what the 250m is, and why the scheduler uses it and not the pod's real usage.

lead.text: CPU is measured in millicores, written `250m`, where 1,000m is one core. A container states a **request**, the amount the scheduler sets aside for it, and a **limit**, the most it may use. The scheduler places a pod only on a node whose unreserved capacity covers the pod's requests, so on a node with 4,000m available it can place 4,000 ÷ 250 = 16 pods that each request 250m.

The scheduler adds up requests and does not look at actual use, which is why requests that are too high waste capacity and requests that are too low let a node be overcommitted. The figure shows the node filling up with the 250m pods and then with 400m pods, 10 of which fill the same space.

afterFigure.text: Limits are enforced differently for the two resources. A container that reaches its CPU limit is *throttled*, slowed but kept running, while one that exceeds its memory limit is *killed*, since memory cannot be taken back. A limit therefore should be set from measurement and not copied from the request.

lead.text: Instead of choosing a replica count by hand, you can set a target for a metric, such as 50 per cent average CPU use, and let the **Horizontal Pod Autoscaler** adjust the replicas. Its rule is desiredReplicas = ceil(currentReplicas × currentMetric ÷ targetMetric). CPU use is measured as a percentage of each pod's *request*, which is why a pod with no request cannot be autoscaled on CPU.

If 4 replicas are running at 80 per cent against a target of 50, the ratio is 80 ÷ 50 = 1.6, so 4 × 1.6 = 6.4, and rounding up gives 7. If 6 replicas run at 30 per cent against a target of 60, the result is 3. The rounding is always up, so the autoscaler leans towards having enough capacity.

afterFigure.text: The autoscaler does nothing when the metric is within roughly 10 per cent of its target, to avoid constant small changes, and it respects a minimum and a maximum that you set.

lead.text: The formula says what the autoscaler wants, not what it can get. It stays within the minimum and maximum you set, and the new pods must still be scheduled, so if the nodes have no unreserved CPU the extra pods stay pending until the cluster adds a node. A rise in replicas is also useless if the real bottleneck is a database that cannot take more connections.

afterFigure.text: The practical lesson is to set requests from measurement so that the percentages mean something, to set a sensible maximum, and to check what lies behind the pods before adding more of them.

blocks.text: Pods in a cluster are created from the same image in every environment, yet the database address in production is not the one used in testing. Something has to differ, and the twelve-factor method says what: the image stays fixed and the configuration is supplied from outside. In Kubernetes that outside is an object in the cluster, and some of it is meant to hold passwords.

Capacity raises a similar question once configuration has left the image, since every pod has to state how much processor time and memory it needs, and those figures decide how many pods fit on a node and how many replicas the autoscaler asks for when load rises. Each of these comes down to a short calculation, and doing it lets you tell in advance whether a cluster has room for what is being asked of it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll explain what protects a Secret, compute how many pods fit on a node by their CPU requests, and calculate the replica count the autoscaler asks for.
intro.whyItMatters: These numbers decide both the cost and the resilience of a cluster.

recap.keyIdea: Configuration lives outside the image, requests decide where pods fit, and the autoscaler sets replicas to the ceiling of current times metric over target.

blocks.text: A ConfigMap or Secret supplies settings from outside the image, and a Secret is only base64-encoded, so access control protects it. The scheduler places pods by summing requests, which is why the number that fit on a node is its capacity divided by one request, and the autoscaler multiplies the current replica count by the ratio of metric to target and rounds up.

lessons.title: Infrastructure as code

reveal.text: No changes. The tool compares the declaration with what exists, and finds no difference to act on.

lead.text: A script of commands records *steps*: create server 1, create server 2, create server 3. Run it twice and it creates six. A **declarative** configuration records the *result*, such as three servers, and a tool such as OpenTofu or Terraform compares that description with what exists and does only what is needed. Applied a second time it finds nothing different and changes nothing.

This is the same idea as the desired state of Kubernetes, applied to everything around the cluster: networks, machines, databases and permissions. Because the description is a text file, it can be kept in version control, reviewed in a pull request and run from the pipeline, like the code it hosts.

afterFigure.text: That is the reason this practice is called infrastructure as code. The infrastructure is changed by changing a file and not by clicking in a console, and the history of the file is the history of the infrastructure.

lead.text: The tool works in two steps. **Plan** compares the configuration with the recorded state and with the real resources, then prints what it would do without doing it. **Apply** carries out the plan. The plan can be read by a person, or posted to a pull request, before anything is changed.

Plan output uses a few symbols. A `+` marks a resource to be created, a `-` one to be destroyed and a `~` one to be changed in place. A `-/+` marks a resource that must be replaced, because some of its settings cannot be changed on a running resource, such as the machine image of a server. The final line counts them. Raising `count` from 3 to 5 gives *Plan: 2 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy*, and a replacement counts as one addition and one destruction.

afterFigure.text: Reading the summary line is the quickest safety check there is. A plan that proposes to destroy a database when you expected to change a tag is a plan to stop and question before applying.

lead.text: To know that `server[0]` in the file is the machine that already exists, the tool keeps a **state** file recording each resource and its real identity. Without it, the tool cannot tell what it already owns, so a lost state means the next plan proposes to create everything again, alongside the resources that already exist. The state is not a cache that can be thrown away.

For a team, the state is stored remotely, in a shared place with *locking*, so that two people cannot apply at once and corrupt it. It also tends to contain sensitive values, such as database passwords the tool created, so it is stored with encryption and with limited access.

afterFigure.text: Reuse comes from **modules**, a set of declarations packaged with **variables** for the parts that differ, so the same module builds a test environment and a production environment with different settings.

lead.text: Suppose someone resizes server 2 by hand in the cloud console, because it was quicker at the time. The files and the state still say small, but the real server is now large. That gap is called **drift**.

The next plan shows it, because plan reads the real resources first. The tool proposes to put the declared setting back, so a hand fix made at midnight can be undone by the next routine apply. The remedy is to make changes in the files, through a pull request, and to run plan regularly to catch drift before it surprises anyone.

afterFigure.text: This is also why plans are reviewed. The plan is the one place where the declared, recorded and real states meet.

blocks.text: A shell script that creates three servers records a list of commands, and running it a second time, after a failed deployment for instance, creates three more, so that six exist where three were wanted. Infrastructure as code records the result instead: a file states that three servers should exist, and a tool such as OpenTofu or Terraform is left to work out what that requires.

Because the file describes an outcome, it can be reviewed and versioned like application code, and the tool can say what it is about to do before it does it. Reading that plan, and knowing what the tool keeps in order to remember which servers are its own, lets you predict what a run will add or destroy and recognise when someone has changed the real infrastructure by hand.

intro.whyItMatters: Everything the cluster runs on can now be reviewed and versioned like application code.

recap.keyIdea: Infrastructure as code declares the end result, and plan compares it with state and reality, so applying twice changes nothing and manual changes show up as drift.

blocks.text: A declarative tool compares the files with its state and with the real resources, and plan prints the additions, changes and destructions it would make before apply does them. State ties declarations to real resources, which is why it is kept safe and shared, and drift is what appears when someone changes the real thing by hand.

reveal.text: It allows 43.2 minutes. The promise leaves a small share of the month uncovered, and that share is the idea of an error budget.

lead.text: With **GitOps**, the desired state of the cluster is kept in a Git repository, and an agent running in the cluster watches that repository and applies any difference, in the same loop of observe, compare and act met in the Kubernetes lesson. The OpenGitOps principles are four: the state is declarative, it is versioned and immutable in Git, it is pulled automatically, and it is continuously reconciled.

The figure compares this with the older push model, where a CI job holds credentials to the cluster and pushes changes in. In the pull model, the credentials stay inside the cluster, since the agent reaches out to Git and nothing reaches in. Rolling back is a Git revert, and every change has an author, a review and a date.

afterFigure.text: Continuous reconciliation also removes drift. If someone edits a Deployment by hand, the agent sees that the cluster no longer matches Git and puts it back, which is the behaviour the previous lesson had to ask people to arrange by running plan regularly.

reveal.text: The agent's job is to make the cluster match Git, and it does not decide which of the two is better.

lead.text: A running service is watched through three kinds of signal. A **metric** is a number measured over time, such as the error rate each minute, and it shows that something changed and when. A **log** is a record of a discrete event, such as a payment timeout, and it says what happened to one thing. A **trace** follows a single request across the services it touches, with the time spent in each step, and it shows where in the path the problem sits.

In the figure the same incident appears three ways. The metric shows the error rate spike, the log shows payments timing out when calling the bank, and the trace shows that of the request's 300 ms, 190 were spent in that bank call. Each one answered a question the others could not.

afterFigure.text: Monitoring watches for failures that were thought of in advance. **Observability** is the property of a system that lets you ask new questions about it without shipping new code, which is what these signals, collected with consistent labels, make possible. OpenTelemetry is a common standard for producing them.

lead.text: A **service level indicator** (SLI) is a measurement of how the service is doing, such as the share of requests that succeed. A **service level objective** (SLO) is the target for it, such as 99.9 per cent over 30 days. The **error budget** is what the objective leaves over: 100 − 99.9 = 0.1 per cent, which over 30 × 24 × 60 = 43,200 minutes is 43,200 × 0.001 = 43.2 minutes of allowed failure.

The figure compares three objectives drawn to the same scale. Raising the target to 99.95 per cent halves the budget to 21.6 minutes, and 99.99 per cent leaves 4.32. Each extra nine costs a great deal, because it leaves the team less room for outages and for the changes that carry risk.

afterFigure.text: A target of 100 per cent is therefore not the safe choice. It leaves no budget, so no change can be shipped, and its cost grows without bound. The Google SRE books use the budget to decide: while there is budget left, the team ships, and when it is spent, the team puts reliability first.

steps.headline: A service has an SLO of 99.8 per cent over 30 days. How many minutes of downtime does its error budget allow?

workedSteps.text: A 30-day month has this many minutes.
The budget is the part of the month the objective leaves over, which is 100 − 99.8 = 0.2 per cent, or 0.002.
Multiply the minutes by that fraction. Give the budget in minutes.

steps.headline: A service has an SLO of 99.97 per cent over 30 days. How many minutes of downtime does its error budget allow?

workedSteps.text: The allowed failure is 100 − 99.97 = 0.03 per cent, which is 0.0003 of the month.
Multiply the 43,200 minutes by it. Give the budget in minutes.

lead.text: With a budget, an outage can be measured as a share of it. A 5.4-minute outage against the 21.6-minute budget spends 5.4 ÷ 21.6 = 25 per cent of it, and two such outages in a month would spend half. The rate at which the budget is being spent is called the burn rate, and an alert on a fast burn is a better page than one on a single failed request.

Alerts should describe symptoms that users feel, such as errors and slow responses, and not causes such as high CPU, which may harm nobody. A page that wakes someone should mean that action is needed now.

afterFigure.text: The budget turns an argument about reliability into arithmetic that product and operations can both read.

reveal.text: Half the budget is gone in one incident, so a second similar one would use it all, and the team would be expected to hold risky changes until the month turned.

blocks.text: A service that promises 99.9 per cent availability over a 30-day month is promising to be down for no more than a small, fixed share of that month's 43,200 minutes. The promise is better read as a budget than as a boast, because the share it leaves over is an allowance of failure that the team may spend on outages and on risky changes, and it frees the team from having to be perfect.

Spending such a budget well needs two other things. The running system has to be kept true to what was declared, which is the job of GitOps, and the team has to be able to see what the system is doing, which is the job of the signals called metrics, logs and traces. With those in place you can say how much failure a target allows, how much of it an outage has used and where to look when something goes wrong.

intro.promise: By the end you'll explain how a GitOps agent keeps a cluster true to Git, choose the right signal for a question, and compute an error budget and how much of it an outage spends.
intro.whyItMatters: A budget is how a team decides how fast it can afford to go.

recap.keyIdea: GitOps pulls desired state from Git into the cluster, three signals say what the system is doing, and an error budget is one minus the objective, spent by outages.

blocks.text: An agent in the cluster reconciles it against Git, which keeps credentials inside and corrects drift. A metric shows that something changed, a log records an event and a trace follows a request, and an SLO of 99.9 per cent over 30 days leaves a budget of 43.2 minutes, which outages are measured against as a percentage.

lead.text: The **software supply chain** is everything that goes into producing and delivering software: your source, the packages it depends on, the base image, the build tools, the pipeline that runs them and the registry that stores the result. In the figure the chain has five stages, and each one has a way in. A key can leak in a commit, a dependency can be replaced by a malicious one, the machine that runs the build can be hijacked, an image in the registry can be swapped, and a deploy key can be stolen.

The pipeline itself is a prime target for two reasons: it holds credentials strong enough to deploy to production, and it runs code from many contributors. The OWASP list of CI/CD risks treats it that way, so the pipeline is not trusted by default.

lead.text: A name such as `node:22`, or a dependency listed as 'any version above 4', can point to something different next month. An attacker, or a careless release, can change what the name means, and the next build quietly picks it up. **Pinning** removes that freedom. For packages, a lock file records the exact version and hash of everything that was installed. For images, a **digest** names the content itself.

A digest is a SHA-256 hash, which is 256 bits, written out in hexadecimal, where each character stands for 4 bits. Referring to an image as node@sha256:… followed by that string of characters names exactly one image. If the content changes by a single byte, the digest changes.

afterFigure.text: Pinning has a cost, because pinned versions go stale and miss security fixes. The remedy is a tool that proposes updates as pull requests, so that updating is a reviewed, tested change and not a silent one.

steps.headline: A SHA-256 digest is 256 bits long and is written in hexadecimal. How many hexadecimal characters is it?

workedSteps.text: Each hexadecimal digit stands for one of 16 values, which is 4 bits.
Divide the digest's bits by the bits in each character. Give the number of characters.
Such a digest names one image exactly, and it does not change unless the content does.

steps.headline: A SHA-512 digest is 512 bits long. How many hexadecimal characters is it?

workedSteps.text: Each hexadecimal character stands for 4 bits.
Divide 512 by 4. Give the number of characters.

lead.text: Git keeps history. A key that was committed and then deleted in the next commit is still in the earlier commit, in every clone and in every fork, so the repository cannot make it secret again. The right response is to **revoke and rotate** the key, meaning that the old one is made invalid and a new one is issued, and then to remove it from the code. Tools that scan commits for keys catch many of these before they reach the shared branch.

Pipelines should hold as little as possible. A deploy job gets a credential that can do only what that job needs, which is **least privilege**, and one that expires within minutes of being issued, so that a stolen credential is worth little by the time it is used. Long-lived keys stored as pipeline variables are the opposite, and they are what an attacker looks for.

afterFigure.text: The same care applies to the code the pipeline runs. A build that executes code from a pull request by an unknown contributor, with access to deploy credentials, hands those credentials to that contributor.

lead.text: Scanning compares the packages in an image with databases of known vulnerabilities. It has to be repeated, because new vulnerabilities are published against software that has not changed, so an image that was clean at build time can be vulnerable a month later. A **software bill of materials** (SBOM) is a machine-readable list of the components inside a built artifact, and it makes that comparison possible for every image at any time, and answers 'are we affected?' within minutes when a new flaw is announced.

Signing completes the chain. The build signs the artifact, and the cluster verifies the signature before it runs it, so an unsigned or altered image is refused. The SLSA specification describes levels of build integrity: at each of its Build levels the build leaves stronger, harder to forge evidence of where an artifact came from, called provenance.

afterFigure.text: Taken together, a pinned digest, a scan, an SBOM and a signature are different answers to the same question: is this the thing we meant to ship?
