lessons.orientation: Identify where a build can be attacked, and apply pinning, least privilege, scanning and signing.
lessons.reviewLabel: Securing the pipeline and the supply chain
lessons.nextAction: You can now describe how a change travels from a commit to a running, observed service, and say where it is at risk.

blocks.text: A build pipeline holds the credentials that can change production, runs code written by every contributor to a repository and downloads packages and base images written by people the team has never met. An attacker who wants to reach production therefore does not need to break into the application itself, since tampering with any one of the things that flow into the build is enough.

Defending that path means taking each stage of the pipeline in turn and asking what it trusts. The answers lead to a short set of habits: pin what the build takes in, keep secrets out of the repository's history, scan and list what is shipped, and sign what is released. Knowing why each one matters lets you decide what to do when a key leaks, when a scan grows stale or when an image arrives unsigned.

intro.promise: By the end you'll name the attack points in a pipeline, compute the length of a digest, and say what to do about a leaked key, a stale scan and an unsigned image.
intro.whyItMatters: This closes the path from commit to production that the course has followed.

recap.keyIdea: Pin what you take in, revoke any secret that has been committed, scan and list what you ship, and sign it so the deploy step can verify it.

blocks.text: Each stage of a pipeline takes in something made elsewhere, so each needs its own control. A digest names exactly one image and is 64 hexadecimal characters for SHA-256, a leaked key must be revoked and rotated because history keeps it, and an SBOM, repeated scans and signed artifacts let you check that what runs is what you meant to ship.

questions.prompt: A team made 15 production deployments in 3 weeks. What is its deployment frequency, in deployments a week?
hints: Pick out what the question gives you and what it asks for.
Frequency is a count divided by a length of time.
Divide 15 by the number of weeks.
questions.onCorrect: 15 deployments over 3 weeks is 5 a week, and the same count over a different window would give a different rate.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies 15 by 3. Frequency divides the count by the period.
That divides the weeks by the deployments. Put the count on top.

questions.prompt: Complete the working: Monday 09:00 to Wednesday 09:00 is 48 hours, and Wednesday 09:00 to 15:00 is 6 more. What is the lead time in hours?
hints: Pick out what the question gives you and what it asks for.
Add the whole days to the extra hours.
questions.onCorrect: Lead time runs from commit to production and counts waiting as well as working time.

misconceptions.feedback: That is only the last part of the interval. The clock started on Monday.
That stops at Wednesday 09:00. The change reached production at 15:00.

questions.prompt: What is the change failure rate, as a percentage, of 6 failing deployments out of 48?
hints: Divide failures by all deployments.
6 ÷ 48 = 0.125. Multiply by 100.
Move the decimal two places.
questions.onCorrect: The rate counts failed deployments against all deployments, so it stays comparable between teams that deploy at different frequencies.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the fraction. Multiply by 100 for a percentage.
That divides 48 by 6. Failures go on top.

questions.prompt: Forty changes ship together and checkout breaks. How many changes are possible causes, before any investigation?
hints: Pick out what the question gives you and what it asks for.
Nothing yet tells you which change is guilty.
Count every change in the release.
questions.onCorrect: Until someone investigates, every change in the batch is a candidate, and combinations of changes can fail where single ones do not.

misconceptions.feedback: That would be true only if the release held one change.
A failure points at the release, not at any one change, so none can be ruled out yet.

questions.prompt: A dashboard shows that 3 of every 20 deployments this month needed a hotfix. Which of the four delivery measures is that share?
hints: It is about deployments that went wrong, not about time.
questions.onCorrect: The share of deployments needing a rollback or hotfix is the change failure rate, here 15 per cent.

misconceptions.feedback: Frequency counts deployments over time. This is a share of them that failed.
Lead time is a duration from commit to production.

questions.prompt: A team moves from monthly releases of about 60 changes to weekly releases of about 15. What should it expect when a release fails?
hints: Think about how many suspects each failing release holds.
The number of changes per release has fallen from 60 to 15.

choices.label: The same search, because the total number of changes is unchanged
No difference, because the failure rate fixes the diagnosis time
A longer search, because releases now happen more often
Fewer changes to search through, and an easier undo

acceptedIdeas: Fewer changes to search through, and an easier undo
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Fewer changes to search through, and an easier undo

questions.onCorrect: Each failing release holds 15 changes at most, so there are fewer suspects and less to undo.

misconceptions.feedback: Total changes are unchanged, but each failure is searched within one release, which is now a quarter the size.
More frequent releases do not lengthen a search; the batch each one holds is what matters.
Failure rate and diagnosis time are separate measures, and batch size affects the second directly.

questions.prompt: A team makes 20 production deployments in 5 weeks. How many deployments a week is that?
hints: Pick out what the question gives you and what it asks for.
Divide the count by the weeks.
Check that your answer is in the unit the question names.
questions.onCorrect: Deployment frequency is a rate, so it can be compared between teams that were measured over different periods.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.prompt: Of a team's 40 deployments, 3 needed a rollback or hotfix. What is the change failure rate as a percentage?
hints: Pick out what the question gives you and what it asks for.
Divide failures by all deployments, then multiply by 100.
Check that your answer is in the unit the question names.
questions.onCorrect: A rate of 7.5 per cent means roughly one deployment in thirteen needed remediation.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the fraction; multiply by 100.
That divides 40 by 3.

questions.prompt: A commit is made on Tuesday at 14:00 and is running in production on Thursday at 08:00. What is the lead time in hours?
hints: Pick out what the question gives you and what it asks for.
Tuesday 14:00 to Wednesday 14:00 is 24 hours.
Then Wednesday 14:00 to Thursday 08:00 is 18 hours.
questions.onCorrect: Lead time counts the whole interval from commit to production, including nights and waiting.

misconceptions.feedback: That is only the last day's part.
That is Tuesday 14:00 to Friday 08:00. The change was live on Thursday.

questions.prompt: You run `git switch -c fix` while on the newest commit of `main`. How many new commits does that create?
hints: Pick out what the question gives you and what it asks for.
Think about what a branch is made of.
Does Git have anything to record yet?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: None: creating a branch adds a label and no commit.

questions.onCorrect: A branch is only a label at a commit, so the graph gains a pointer and no commit until you commit on it.

misconceptions.feedback: A commit records a change, and none has been made yet.

questions.prompt: In Git, a branch is a movable ___ to a commit. What word fills the gap?
hints: The branch holds only an address, not any files.
questions.onCorrect: A branch is just a name that points at one commit, and it moves forward when you commit while it is checked out.

misconceptions.feedback: A copy would hold the files. A branch holds none and costs almost nothing to create.

questions.prompt: 6 developers merge 12 commits a day in total. A branch lives 15 working days. How many commits does main gain?
hints: Pick out what the question gives you and what it asks for.
Multiply the daily total by the days.
questions.onCorrect: The branch has missed 180 commits, each a chance of disagreeing with its own changes.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a single day's commits. The branch lives 15 days.
That uses 6 × 15. Each developer merges 2 commits a day.

questions.prompt: 4 developers each merge 3 commits a day, and a branch lives 5 working days. How many commits does main gain?
hints: Pick out what the question gives you and what it asks for.
First find the commits per day for the whole team.
12 per day over 5 days.
questions.onCorrect: The count grows with both the team size and the time, so short branches matter more on larger teams.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one day's commits only.
That multiplies 3 by 5 and leaves out the 4 developers.

questions.prompt: A developer has a feature that will take three weeks and wants to merge it to the trunk every day without exposing it to users. Which practice allows this?
hints: The code must be in the trunk but not reachable by users.

choices.label: Keep the branch private until the feature is finished
Skip code review for unfinished work
Hide the feature behind a feature flag
Rebase the branch once a month

acceptedIdeas: Hide the feature behind a feature flag
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Hide the feature behind a feature flag

questions.onCorrect: A flag separates integrating code from releasing it, so each small piece can merge while the feature stays off.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the long-lived branch the lesson warned about, and it only delays the integration problem.
Review is a gate on the trunk and is not what hides the feature from users.
A rebase once a month leaves the branch behind for weeks.

questions.prompt: On a team of 6 developers, each merges 2 commits a day to main, and no branch may live longer than 2 working days. How many commits can main gain while one branch is open?
hints: Pick out what the question gives you and what it asks for.
Daily total first: 6 × 2.
Then multiply by 2 days.
questions.onCorrect: A two-day limit keeps the reconciliation small enough to understand in one sitting.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one day. The branch lives 2 days.
That is the fifteen-day figure.

questions.prompt: A branch lives 10 working days while 8 developers each merge 3 commits a day to main. How many commits has main gained?
hints: Pick out what the question gives you and what it asks for.
Commits per day: 8 × 3.
Check that your answer is in the unit the question names.
questions.onCorrect: The drift is team size times commit rate times days, so each factor scales it linearly.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a single day's commits.
That multiplies 3 by 10 and leaves out the 8 developers.

questions.prompt: Two branches changed the same lines of a file, and Git stops a merge and asks a person to decide. What is this called?
hints: It is reported at the moment two branches are joined.
questions.onCorrect: A conflict is a symptom of the time two changes spent apart, and trunk-based development keeps that time short.

misconceptions.feedback: A pull request is a proposal to merge. The disagreement over the same lines is called something else.

questions.prompt: What does creating a branch in Git do?
hints: Recall the first figure: what is added to the graph?

choices.label: It copies every file to a new folder
It locks the main branch against new commits
It uploads the code to a server
It creates a new movable pointer to a commit

acceptedIdeas: It creates a new movable pointer to a commit
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It creates a new movable pointer to a commit

questions.onCorrect: The pointer moves forward when you commit on the branch, and nothing else about the project is duplicated.

misconceptions.feedback: Git stores snapshots by content, and no copy of the files is made when a branch appears.
Other people can still commit to main while you work on a branch.
Creating a branch is local and involves no server.

questions.prompt: Lint 2, build 5, unit tests 8, integration tests 12 and deploy 3 minutes, one after another. How many minutes is the pipeline?
hints: Pick out what the question gives you and what it asks for.
Stages in sequence add.
questions.onCorrect: With no overlap the total is the sum, and the author learns of a failure only as late as its stage's position allows.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the longest stage only; in sequence all of them count.

questions.prompt: A pipeline builds for 4 minutes, then runs lint (2 minutes), unit tests (11) and integration tests (8) side by side, then deploys to staging in 3. How many minutes does the pipeline take?
hints: Pick out what the question gives you and what it asks for.
Count each parallel group once, at its longest member.
questions.onCorrect: Parallel stages cost only as much as the slowest, so shortening a stage that is not the slowest saves nothing.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds all five stages as if they ran in sequence.
That leaves out one of the sequential parts. Build and deploy still count.

questions.prompt: A 32-minute test suite is split into 4 equal shards run in parallel. How many minutes does the stage take, ignoring set-up?
hints: Pick out what the question gives you and what it asks for.
Divide the work between the shards.
questions.onCorrect: A stage with balanced shards lasts as long as one shard, though set-up time per shard limits how far splitting can go.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the unsharded time. Shards share the work.
That multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.prompt: Build 4 minutes, then lint 1, unit tests 6 and integration tests 9 in parallel, then deploy 2. How many minutes does the pipeline take?
hints: Pick out what the question gives you and what it asks for.
The parallel group counts once.
questions.onCorrect: The integration tests set the duration of the middle group, so speeding up lint would not shorten the pipeline.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds lint and unit tests to the sum. They finish inside the 9 minutes.
That is only the middle group.

questions.prompt: What is the versioned, never-modified output of the build stage called, which every later stage and environment reuses? Give the two-word name.
hints: It has two words, and the second names the thing that is built and kept.
questions.onCorrect: Promoting one artifact through each environment guarantees that production runs what the tests saw.

misconceptions.feedback: A container is one kind of artifact, but the general name covers any versioned build output.

questions.prompt: A 32-minute test suite is split into 4 shards that run in parallel, but unevenly: one shard holds 14 minutes of tests and the other three hold 6 minutes each. How many minutes does the stage take?
hints: Pick out what the question gives you and what it asks for.
The stage ends when the last shard ends.
Which shard is longest?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The longest shard is 14 minutes, so the stage takes 14 minutes.

questions.onCorrect: Shard balance sets the real gain, because the slowest shard decides when the stage finishes.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the time if the shards were balanced; these are not.
That is the unsharded time. The split does help, just not to 8.

questions.prompt: Build takes 6 minutes. Lint (3), unit tests (10) and integration tests (15) then run in parallel, and deploy takes 4. How many minutes does the pipeline take?
hints: Pick out what the question gives you and what it asks for.
Find the longest of the parallel stages.
Check that your answer is in the unit the question names.
questions.onCorrect: Only the slowest parallel stage is counted, which is why teams look for the longest chain before they optimise anything.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds all five stages in sequence.
That counts the unit tests (10) as the longest. Integration tests take 15.

questions.prompt: A 45-minute test suite is split into 5 balanced shards that run in parallel. How many minutes does the stage take, ignoring set-up?
hints: Pick out what the question gives you and what it asks for.
Divide the work evenly.
Check that your answer is in the unit the question names.
questions.onCorrect: Balanced shards finish together, so the stage lasts as long as one of them.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies. Parallel shards share the work.
That subtracts 5 from 45.

questions.prompt: Which check belongs first in a pipeline?
hints: Early failure is worth most when it is cheap.

choices.label: A manual approval
The slowest end-to-end test
The cheapest check that catches the most common failures
Production deployment

acceptedIdeas: The cheapest check that catches the most common failures
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The cheapest check that catches the most common failures

questions.onCorrect: Cheap, quick checks give the author feedback while they still remember the change, and they spare the slow stages from running on a broken build.

misconceptions.feedback: Running the slowest test first makes every failure wait for it.
Deploying is the last step, after the checks that decide whether it should happen.
An approval is slow and depends on a person, so it belongs after the automatic checks.

questions.prompt: A service has 18 instances, and a rolling update replaces 3 at a time. How many batches does the update need?
hints: Pick out what the question gives you and what it asks for.
Each batch replaces 3 instances.
questions.onCorrect: Only 3 of 18 instances are out of service at once, which is why a rolling update needs no spare environment.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies. Each batch removes instances from the total.
That is the batch size, not the number of batches.

questions.prompt: A service receives 1,500 requests a second and a canary gets 4 per cent. How many requests a second reach the canary?
hints: Pick out what the question gives you and what it asks for.
Write 4 per cent as 0.04.
questions.onCorrect: The canary sees real traffic, but only a twenty-fifth of it, so most users are unaffected if it fails.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the traffic that stays on the old version.
That multiplies by 4 instead of taking 4 per cent.

questions.prompt: A canary receives 300 requests a second and fails on 1 per cent of them. How many errors a second is that?
hints: Pick out what the question gives you and what it asks for.
The rate applies to the canary's own traffic.
questions.onCorrect: The error rate, not the count, is what is compared with the old version.

misconceptions.feedback: That takes 10 per cent of 300; the failure rate is 1 per cent.
That takes 1 per cent of 900, the total.

questions.prompt: A release drops the column `customer_name` from a database table and moves its data into a new table. It fails, and the team redeploys the old code. What happens to the dropped column and its data?
hints: Think about what a deployment changes and what it leaves alone.

choices.label: It returns, because the old code recreates the column
It returns once the traffic is switched back
It is restored automatically from the canary
It is still gone, because redeploying code does not undo a database change

acceptedIdeas: It is still gone, because redeploying code does not undo a database change
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is still gone, because redeploying code does not undo a database change

questions.onCorrect: A schema change lives in the database, so reversing it needs a backup or a new migration, not a code rollback.

misconceptions.feedback: Old code can ask for a column but cannot rebuild the data that was dropped.
Traffic moves between versions of code and has no effect on stored data.
A canary is a share of traffic and keeps no copy of the database.

questions.prompt: What is the name for a condition in the code that keeps a finished feature switched off for users until someone turns it on, so that code can be deployed without being released?
hints: It is a flag or toggle in the code.
questions.onCorrect: Turning a flag off is the fastest rollback, but a flag left behind after release becomes debt.

misconceptions.feedback: A canary is a share of real traffic. The code-level switch is called something else.

questions.prompt: A service runs on 20 instances and is released by blue-green deployment. At the moment of the switch, both the live environment and the new one are running at full size. How many instances are running in total?
hints: Pick out what the question gives you and what it asks for.
Two environments, each the size of production.
questions.onCorrect: The spare environment is what makes the switch and the rollback instant, and its cost is the reason blue-green is not free.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a single environment. Blue-green needs both at the switch.
That halves the figure instead of doubling it.

questions.prompt: A service receives 4,000 requests a second and a canary is given 3 per cent. How many requests a second reach the canary?
hints: Pick out what the question gives you and what it asks for.
Write 3 per cent as 0.03.
Check that your answer is in the unit the question names.
questions.onCorrect: A small share keeps the blast radius small while still exposing the version to real traffic.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the traffic left on the old version.
That multiplies by 3.

questions.prompt: A rolling update replaces 12 instances 3 at a time. How many batches does it need?
hints: Pick out what the question gives you and what it asks for.
Divide the instances by the batch size.
Check that your answer is in the unit the question names.
questions.onCorrect: Each batch is a point where the update can be stopped if the new version misbehaves.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies instead of dividing.
That is the batch size.

questions.prompt: Which strategy needs capacity for two full production environments at the switch?
hints: Which strategy keeps a whole idle copy ready?

choices.label: Rolling update
Feature flag
Blue-green deployment
Canary release

questions.onCorrect: The idle environment is why the switch and the rollback are instant, and why the strategy costs more to run.

misconceptions.feedback: A rolling update replaces instances in place and needs only a little spare capacity.
A canary adds a few instances for a small share of traffic.
A flag is a condition in the code and needs no extra servers.

questions.prompt: Namespaces limit what a process can see. Which Linux kernel feature limits what it can use, such as the memory or processor time a container is allowed?
hints: Namespaces limit what a process can see. The other feature limits what it can use.
questions.onCorrect: The kernel enforces cgroup limits, so a container that exceeds its memory is stopped without affecting its neighbours.

misconceptions.feedback: Namespaces limit what a process can see, not how much it can use.
Namespaces limit what a process can see, not how much it can use.

questions.prompt: Which part of the operating system do all containers on a host share?
hints: A virtual machine has its own copy of this part.
questions.onCorrect: Sharing the kernel makes containers start in milliseconds and means a kernel flaw affects them all.

misconceptions.feedback: Each container brings its own files, so what they share is narrower: the core that manages hardware and runs processes.
The files differ per container, so the shared part is narrower than the whole operating system: its core.

questions.prompt: One 300 MB image has three containers, each with a 6 MB writable layer. How many MB of disk do they use together?
hints: Pick out what the question gives you and what it asks for.
The image is stored once.
questions.onCorrect: Sharing the read-only layers is what makes starting many containers cheap in disk as well as in time.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the image three times. Its layers are shared.
That is only the writable layers; the image counts as well.

questions.prompt: One 80 MB image has four containers, each with a 2 MB writable layer. How many MB of disk do they use together?
hints: Pick out what the question gives you and what it asks for.
The image counts once.
questions.onCorrect: Each extra container costs only its writable layer, here 2 MB.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the image four times.
That leaves out the 80 MB image.

questions.prompt: You start one image three times and then delete one container. How many copies of the image remain on the host?
hints: Pick out what the question gives you and what it asks for.
Is the image part of the container?
Deleting a container removes only its writable layer.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One: the image was never removed.

questions.onCorrect: The image is a separate stored template, so deleting a container leaves it and every other container untouched.

misconceptions.feedback: The image is not part of the container, so it is not removed with it.
That is the number of containers still left, not images.

questions.prompt: A container is limited to 256 MiB of memory and its program tries to use 300 MiB. What happens?
hints: Think of a cgroup as a limit the kernel enforces.

choices.label: The kernel stops the process for exceeding its limit
The kernel lets it borrow memory from the other containers
The host restarts to make room
The image is deleted and rebuilt

acceptedIdeas: The kernel stops the process for exceeding its limit
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The kernel stops the process for exceeding its limit

questions.onCorrect: The memory limit protects the other containers, which carry on unaffected.

misconceptions.feedback: Borrowing would defeat the limit, whose purpose is to protect the others.
The limit applies to the container, and the host stays up.
The image is a read-only template and is not touched by a running process.

questions.prompt: One 150 MB image has five containers, each with a 10 MB writable layer. How many MB of disk do they use together?
hints: Pick out what the question gives you and what it asks for.
Count the image once and the writable layers five times.
Check that your answer is in the unit the question names.
questions.onCorrect: A host can run many containers from one image for little more than the cost of the image itself.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the image five times.
That leaves out the 150 MB image.

questions.prompt: Which Linux feature gives a container its own process list and network, limiting what it can see?
hints: One feature limits what a process can see; the other limits what it can use.

choices.label: hypervisors
namespaces
cgroups
registries

questions.onCorrect: Namespaces separate the views, and cgroups separate the resources, and a container needs both.

misconceptions.feedback: Cgroups limit what a process can use, such as memory.
A hypervisor belongs to virtual machines, not containers.
A registry stores images and has no effect on what a process sees.

questions.prompt: What is the server called that stores images under names and versions so hosts can pull them?
hints: Hosts pull images from it before running them.
questions.onCorrect: A host must pull an image from a registry before it can start a container from it.

misconceptions.feedback: A repository is one named collection of images. Name the server that holds such collections.

questions.prompt: Dockerfile: `FROM node:22`; `COPY package.json .`; `RUN npm ci`; `COPY src ./src`; `CMD ["node","src/app.js"]`. After editing only `src/app.js`, how many of the five instructions are rebuilt?
hints: A layer is reused if it and everything before it are unchanged.
Which is the first instruction affected by the edit?
Everything from that instruction onward is rebuilt.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: COPY src ./src and CMD are rebuilt, so 2.

questions.onCorrect: The edit first touches COPY src, and CMD follows it, so the dependency install stays cached.

misconceptions.feedback: The install comes before the copy of the source, so it is not affected by an edit to the source.
Only layers from the first changed one onward are rebuilt.

questions.prompt: A Dockerfile has five instructions: `FROM node:22`, `COPY . .`, `RUN npm ci`, `RUN npm run build` and `CMD ["node","dist/app.js"]`. You edit only `src/app.js` and build again. How many of the five instructions are rebuilt?
hints: Pick out what the question gives you and what it asks for.
Which instruction first sees the edited file?
Everything after it is rebuilt.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: COPY . ., RUN npm ci, RUN npm run build and CMD are rebuilt, so 4.

questions.onCorrect: Copying everything first means any edit invalidates the install that follows.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the copy, and the layers after it are rebuilt too.
`FROM` is unchanged, so it is reused.

questions.prompt: A build stage is 1,100 MB and the shipped final stage is 140 MB. How many MB smaller is the shipped image than the build stage?
hints: Pick out what the question gives you and what it asks for.
Subtract the smaller from the larger.
questions.onCorrect: The tools stay in the build stage, and the shipped image carries only what the app needs to run.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two sizes.
That is the shipped size, not the saving.

questions.prompt: A build stage is 900 MB and the shipped final stage is 120 MB. How many MB smaller is the shipped image?
hints: Pick out what the question gives you and what it asks for.
Subtract.
questions.onCorrect: A smaller image is faster to pull and has fewer parts to attack.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two sizes.
That is the shipped size.

questions.prompt: Which keyword names a stage so that a later stage can copy from it, as in `FROM golang ___ build`?
hints: It is a two-letter word that precedes the stage name.
questions.onCorrect: The name given with `AS` is what `COPY --from` refers to.

misconceptions.feedback: `FROM` starts every stage. The missing word sits between the image name and the stage name.

questions.prompt: A Dockerfile copies a .env file containing a password into the image in step 2, and step 3 runs rm to delete it. Someone pulls the finished image. Can the password be recovered?
hints: Think about whether a layer can be edited after it is made.

choices.label: Only if the image is rebuilt with the cache on
No, because layers are encrypted
No, because the delete removes it from the image
Yes, because the earlier layer still holds the file

acceptedIdeas: Yes, because the earlier layer still holds the file
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes, because the earlier layer still holds the file

questions.onCorrect: The later layer only hides the file, so the earlier layer remains in the image and its contents can be extracted.

misconceptions.feedback: A delete adds a new layer and leaves the earlier layers as they were.
Layers are not encrypted, and the content is readable.
The cache affects build speed and has no bearing on what the finished image contains.

questions.prompt: A build stage is 1,500 MB and the final stage that is shipped is 200 MB. How many MB smaller is the shipped image than the build stage?
hints: Pick out what the question gives you and what it asks for.
Subtract the shipped size from the build stage's size.
Check that your answer is in the unit the question names.
questions.onCorrect: Only the final stage is pushed, so the build stage's size does not reach the registry.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two.
That is the shipped size.

questions.prompt: Dockerfile: `FROM node:22`; `WORKDIR /app`; `COPY package.json .`; `RUN npm ci`; `COPY src ./src`; `RUN npm run build`. You change `package.json` only. How many of the six instructions are rebuilt?
hints: Pick out what the question gives you and what it asks for.
Find the first instruction whose inputs changed.
Count it and every instruction after it.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: `COPY package.json`, `npm ci`, `COPY src` and `npm run build` are rebuilt, so 4.

questions.onCorrect: The package file feeds the third instruction, so everything from there on is rebuilt.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of instructions before the changed one, which are reused.
A changed layer invalidates all later layers as well.

questions.prompt: Which base-image reference makes a build most repeatable?
hints: Which of these names one exact image that cannot move?

choices.label: node:22 with the cache switched on

misconceptions.feedback: The B stands for a word used for a manufacturer's parts list, not for building.

questions.prompt: An image was scanned at build time and had no known vulnerabilities. Three weeks later a new vulnerability is published for one of its packages, and nothing in the image has changed. Does the earlier scan result still hold?
hints: The software is unchanged, but what is known about it has changed.

choices.label: Yes, because the image has not changed
No, because the digest has changed
Yes, because scanning at build time is the only scan needed
No, because new vulnerabilities are published against unchanged software, so scans must repeat

acceptedIdeas: No, because new vulnerabilities are published against unchanged software, so scans must repeat
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, because new vulnerabilities are published against unchanged software, so scans must repeat

questions.onCorrect: This is why teams rescan images in the registry and in use, and keep an SBOM to make that cheap.

misconceptions.feedback: The scan reflects what was known then, and the image did not stay safe merely by staying the same.
A single scan cannot know about flaws found afterwards.
The digest does not change unless the content does.

questions.prompt: A SHA-384 digest is 384 bits long, and each hexadecimal character stands for 4 bits. How many hexadecimal characters is it?
hints: Pick out what the question gives you and what it asks for.
Divide the bits by 4.
Check that your answer is in the unit the question names.
questions.onCorrect: The digest names the content, and a longer digest makes a collision correspondingly less likely.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of bits.
That divides by 8, the bits in a byte, which would give bytes and not characters.

questions.prompt: What is the SHA-256 hash of an image's content, used to name exactly one image, called?
hints: Unlike a tag, it cannot be moved.
questions.onCorrect: Pinning a base image by digest means a build cannot silently pick up a different image.

misconceptions.feedback: A tag is a label that can be moved to another image, so it does not name one exactly.

questions.prompt: Which credential is best for a deploy job in a pipeline?
hints: Think of what an attacker who steals it can do, and for how long.

choices.label: A personal login borrowed from a developer
The same key for every job, so it is easy to rotate
A long-lived administrator key stored as a pipeline variable
A short-lived credential that can only do what that job needs

acceptedIdeas: A short-lived credential that can only do what that job needs
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A short-lived credential that can only do what that job needs

questions.onCorrect: If it is stolen, it can do little and expires soon, which limits the damage.

misconceptions.feedback: An administrator key that does not expire is worth the most to an attacker.
A personal login ties the pipeline to a person and carries all of that person's access.
One key for every job means every job's compromise exposes every capability.

questions.prompt: A team releases forty changes together on a Friday afternoon, and checkout breaks right after the release. Before anyone investigates, which changes could be responsible?
hints: Nothing in the failure itself names the change that caused it.
questions.onCorrect: Until someone investigates, all forty are candidates, and two changes together can fail where neither does alone.

acceptedIdeas: Any of the forty, alone or in combination with another
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Any of the forty, alone or in combination with another

misconceptions.feedback: All forty went live in the same release, so the order in which they were merged says nothing about which one is at fault.
A change elsewhere, such as to a shared library or a configuration value, can break checkout without touching its code, so those changes are suspects too.
Testing each change on its own cannot catch a fault that appears only when two changes run together, and tests miss some faults in any case.

choices.label: None of them, since each change was tested on its own
Any of the forty, alone or in combination with another
Only the last change merged before the release
Only the changes that touched the checkout code

questions.prompt: You are on the newest commit of `main` and run `git switch -c fix`, which creates a branch called `fix` and moves you onto it. What does the command add to the repository's history?
hints: Think about how long the command takes, even in a very large project.
questions.onCorrect: A branch is only a label at a commit, so the graph gains a pointer and no commit until you commit on fix.

acceptedIdeas: No new commit, only a new name for the commit you are on
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No new commit, only a new name for the commit you are on

misconceptions.feedback: Git records a commit only when you commit something, and creating a branch changes no files, so there is nothing for a new commit to hold.
The commits on main are stored once and fix can share them, so nothing is copied, which is why the command is instant even in a large project.

choices.label: No new commit, only a new name for the commit you are on
One new commit that marks where fix begins
A copy of every commit on main, stored under the name fix

questions.prompt: A pipeline runs five stages one after another: lint takes 2 minutes, build 5, unit tests 8, integration tests 12 and deploy to staging 3. Roughly how long does the whole pipeline take?
hints: Each stage starts only when the one before it has finished.
questions.onCorrect: Stages in sequence add to 2 + 5 + 8 + 12 + 3 = 30 minutes, so a failure in a late stage reaches its author only after most of that time.

acceptedIdeas: About 30 minutes, the stage times added together
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 30 minutes, the stage times added together

misconceptions.feedback: The longest stage sets the time only when stages run side by side. Here each stage waits for the one before it, so their times add.
An average describes a typical stage, but the pipeline has to wait for all five in turn, so their times add.

choices.label: About 6 minutes, the length of an average stage
About 30 minutes, the stage times added together
About 12 minutes, the length of the longest stage

questions.prompt: A host runs ten containers, and each one believes it has its own filesystem and its own process list. Which part of the operating system do all ten still share?
hints: A virtual machine has its own copy of this part.
questions.onCorrect: Sharing the kernel makes containers start in milliseconds and means a kernel flaw affects them all.

acceptedIdeas: The kernel, which runs every process on the host
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The kernel, which runs every process on the host

misconceptions.feedback: A virtual machine carries its own operating system and kernel. A container is a process on the host, so it runs on the host's kernel.
Each container sees a filesystem of its own built from its image, so its files are kept apart from the others'.

choices.label: Their files, because all ten write to one shared directory
The kernel, which runs every process on the host
Nothing, because each container carries a complete operating system of its own

questions.prompt: You start one image three times, so three containers exist, and then delete one of the containers. What happens to the image?
hints: Is the image part of the container, or something the container was started from?
questions.onCorrect: The image is a separate stored template, so deleting a container leaves it and every other container untouched.

acceptedIdeas: It stays on the host unchanged, and the other two containers keep running
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It stays on the host unchanged, and the other two containers keep running

misconceptions.feedback: The image is a separate stored template. Deleting a container removes only that container's writable layer.
A container's writes go into its own writable layer and never into the image, so the image holds exactly what it held before.
An image stays on the host until someone deletes it on purpose, whether or not any container is running from it.

choices.label: It loses the files that the deleted container wrote
It is kept only until the other two containers stop
It stays on the host unchanged, and the other two containers keep running
It is deleted along with the container

questions.prompt: A Dockerfile has five instructions: `FROM node:22`, then `COPY package.json .`, then `RUN npm ci`, then `COPY src ./src`, and finally `CMD ["node","src/app.js"]`. You edit only `src/app.js` and build again. Which instructions does the builder run again?
hints: Find the first instruction that the edit affects.
Each layer sits on top of the layer before it.
questions.onCorrect: The edit first touches COPY src, and CMD follows it, so the dependency install stays cached.

acceptedIdeas: COPY src ./src and every instruction after it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: COPY src ./src and every instruction after it

misconceptions.feedback: Each layer is built on top of the one before it, so once COPY src ./src produces a new layer, the CMD layer above it has to be made again too.
The base image, `package.json` and the dependency install all come before the edited file and are unchanged, so the builder reuses them from its cache.
The builder checks the files an instruction copies as well as the instruction's text, so a changed `src/app.js` makes `COPY src ./src` run again.

choices.label: All five, starting again from `FROM`
None, because the Dockerfile itself has not changed
COPY src ./src and every instruction after it
Only COPY src ./src, the instruction that copies the edited file

questions.prompt: The command `docker run -p 8080:80 nginx` starts a web server that listens on port 80 inside its container. At which address can a browser on the host reach it?
hints: The flag `-p` joins two port numbers, one on each side of the container's boundary.
questions.onCorrect: The host port is the first number, and the container's port 80 is only reachable through it.

misconceptions.feedback: Port 80 belongs to the container's own network. The `-p` flag opens port 8080 on the host and passes its traffic through to port 80 inside.
A container's ports are private by default, and changing that is exactly what `-p` does: it publishes a port of the container on the host.

choices.label: localhost:8080
Neither, because a container's ports can never be reached from the host
localhost:80, the port the server listens on

questions.prompt: Two containers, web and db, are started by a compose file and share one network. The web program needs to connect to the database. What should it use as the database's address?
hints: Container addresses change every time a container is recreated.
questions.onCorrect: The name stays the same when the database container is recreated, while its address changes.

misconceptions.feedback: Each container has its own network, so localhost inside web means web itself, where no database is listening.
That address works only until the database container is recreated and gets a new one, so a program that stores it will eventually lose the database.

choices.label: The database container's current IP address, looked up after it starts
The service name, db
localhost, since both containers run on the same host

questions.prompt: You want three nginx containers on one host, each reachable from a browser, and each listens on port 80 inside its container. How must their ports be published?
hints: A host port can lead to one container.
questions.onCorrect: Container ports may repeat because each container has a network of its own, but host ports must be distinct.

acceptedIdeas: On three different host ports, each mapped to port 80 in its own container
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: On three different host ports, each mapped to port 80 in its own container

misconceptions.feedback: A host port can lead to only one container, so a second container asking for host port 80 is refused.
A published port leads to a single container. Spreading traffic over several needs a load balancer, which `-p` does not provide.
Each container has its own network, so all three can listen on port 80 inside. Only the host side of each mapping has to differ.

choices.label: All three on host port 80, since that is the port they listen on
Not at all, because three servers cannot all listen on port 80
On one host port, which shares its traffic among the three
On three different host ports, each mapped to port 80 in its own container

questions.prompt: A Deployment, the Kubernetes object that says how many copies of a program should run, declares 5 replicas, and 3 of those copies, called pods, are running. What will Kubernetes do?
hints: Compare what is declared with what is running.
questions.onCorrect: The controller acts on the difference, so the count it creates is desired minus observed.

acceptedIdeas: Create 2 more pods, so that 5 are running
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Create 2 more pods, so that 5 are running

misconceptions.feedback: The 3 running pods already count towards the 5, so the controller adds only the difference.
A controller keeps comparing what is declared with what exists, so it acts on the shortfall without anyone typing a command.
The declaration is what the cluster works towards, and it changes only when someone edits it.

choices.label: Create 5 new pods, replacing the 3 that are running
Create 2 more pods, so that 5 are running
Nothing, until someone runs a command to start more
Lower the declared count to 3, to match what exists

questions.prompt: A Service has the selector `app=web`. Four pods exist: one labelled `app=web` and ready, one labelled `app=web` and not yet ready, one labelled `app=db` and ready, and another labelled `app=web` and ready. Which pods receive traffic from the Service?
hints: Think about both the label and whether the pod is ready.
questions.onCorrect: Only ready pods that match the selector are used, so a pod still starting is skipped.

acceptedIdeas: The two labelled `app=web` that are ready
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The two labelled app=web that are ready

misconceptions.feedback: A Service sends traffic only to pods whose labels match its selector, so the `app=db` pod is never chosen.
Matching the label is not enough on its own, since a pod that is not yet ready is left out until it is.
Readiness is checked only among the pods the selector matches, and the `app=db` pod does not match `app=web`.

choices.label: The three that are ready
The two labelled `app=web` that are ready
All four, because they are all in the cluster
The three labelled `app=web`

questions.prompt: A node has 4,000m of allocatable CPU, where m means a thousandth of a CPU core, and each pod asks the scheduler for 250m. Roughly how many such pods can the scheduler place on the node by CPU?
hints: 4,000m is four whole cores.
questions.onCorrect: The scheduler adds up requests, so the number that fit depends on what pods ask for and not on their real use.

misconceptions.feedback: A pod asking for 250m needs only a quarter of a core, so four such pods fit on each core.
250 is one pod's request in millicores, not a count of pods. Dividing the node's 4,000m by 250m gives the number that fit.
The scheduler counts what pods request, not what they use, and stops placing them once the requests add up to the node's capacity.

choices.label: About 250
About 4, one for each core
As many as are needed, since pods rarely use all they ask for
About 16

questions.prompt: A configuration declares `count = 3` servers, and three servers already exist and match it exactly. You run plan. What does it propose?
hints: The file says what should exist, not what to do.
questions.onCorrect: A declarative tool acts on differences, so applying the same configuration again changes nothing.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what a script of commands would do on a second run. A declarative tool compares the file with what exists, and three of the three already exist.
The tool replaces a resource only when its declaration differs from what exists, and here nothing differs.

choices.label: Adding three more servers, since the file asks for three
Replacing the three servers with fresh copies
No changes

questions.prompt: A service promises to be available 99.9 per cent of the time over a 30-day month, which has 43,200 minutes. Roughly how much downtime does that promise allow in the month?
hints: The promise leaves 0.1 per cent of the month uncovered.
questions.onCorrect: The 0.1 per cent left over by the objective is the budget, 43.2 minutes in a 30-day month.

misconceptions.feedback: 99.9 per cent leaves 0.1 per cent of the month uncovered, and 0.1 per cent of 43,200 minutes is 43.2 minutes.
0.1 per cent of 43,200 minutes is 43.2 minutes, not 43 seconds, so the allowance is sixty times larger than that.
43 hours would be about 6 per cent of the month. The 0.1 per cent the promise leaves is 43,200 × 0.001 = 43.2 minutes.

choices.label: About three-quarters of an hour
About 43 seconds
None at all
About 43 hours

flashcards.front: What is the change failure rate of 5 failing deployments out of 25?
flashcards.back: 5 ÷ 25 is 0.2, which is 20 per cent, a share of all deployments.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 5 ÷ 25 is 0.2, which is 20 per cent, a share of all deployments.

flashcards.front: Which measure is the time from a commit to that commit running in production?
flashcards.back: It is the lead time for changes, and it begins at the commit rather than at the first line of code.

flashcards.front: Why does shipping smaller batches usually lower risk?
flashcards.back: A failure in a small release has few candidate causes and a cheap undo, so it is found and reversed faster.

flashcards.front: In Git, what is a branch?
flashcards.back: It is a movable pointer to one commit, so creating it copies no files.

flashcards.front: A branch lives 4 days while 5 developers each merge 2 commits a day. How many commits does main gain?
flashcards.back: 5 × 2 × 4 = 40 commits that the branch has not seen.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 5 × 2 × 4 = 40 commits that the branch has not seen.

flashcards.front: Why is a merge conflict called a symptom of delayed integration?
flashcards.back: The longer two branches stay apart, the more likely they edit the same lines, so conflicts measure the delay.

flashcards.front: What is a build artifact?
flashcards.back: It is the versioned, unmodified output of the build, reused by every later stage so what was tested is what ships.

flashcards.front: Build 3 minutes, then two checks of 4 and 7 minutes in parallel. How many minutes in total?
flashcards.back: 3 + 7 = 10, because the parallel pair lasts as long as the slower check.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 3 + 7 = 10, because the parallel pair lasts as long as the slower check.

flashcards.front: Why should a pipeline put cheap, fast checks first?
flashcards.back: A failure is then reported within minutes, while the author still remembers the change, and slow stages are not run on a broken build.

flashcards.front: What does a canary release do?
flashcards.back: It sends a small share of real traffic to the new version and compares its error rate with the old version's before widening.

flashcards.front: A service gets 1,000 requests a second and a canary gets 10 per cent. How many requests a second reach the canary?
flashcards.back: 10 per cent of 1,000 is 100 requests a second.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 10 per cent of 1,000 is 100 requests a second.

flashcards.front: What name is given to making a schema change in stages by adding the new column before dropping the old one?
flashcards.back: It is expand then contract, and it keeps rollback possible while both versions of the code run.

flashcards.front: Which part of the system do containers on one host share?
flashcards.back: They share the host kernel, so a container starts in milliseconds but a kernel flaw affects them all.

flashcards.front: One 120 MB image has 2 containers, each with a 4 MB writable layer. How many MB of disk is that?
flashcards.back: 120 + 2 × 4 = 128 MB, because the image is stored once.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 120 + 2 × 4 = 128 MB, because the image is stored once.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between an image and a container?
flashcards.back: An image is a stored read-only template, and a container is a running instance with a writable layer.

flashcards.front: In a multi-stage build, which keyword names a stage so it can be copied from later?
flashcards.back: The word `AS` names the stage, and `COPY --from` takes files out of it.

flashcards.front: A build stage is 800 MB and the shipped stage is 150 MB. How many MB is the saving?
Why should `COPY package.json` and `RUN npm ci` come before `COPY src` in a Dockerfile?
flashcards.back: The dependency layers then stay cached when only source files change, so the slow install is not repeated.

flashcards.front: In `-p 8080:80`, which number is the host's port?
flashcards.back: The host port is written first, so 8080 is the host's port and 80 the container's.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The host port is written first, so 8080 is the host's port and 80 the container's.

flashcards.front: What name is given to storage that survives a container being removed?
flashcards.back: A volume is stored outside the container's writable layer, so it outlives the container.

flashcards.front: Why do containers on one user-defined network reach each other by service name?
flashcards.back: Docker resolves the name to the container's current address, which changes whenever the container is recreated.

flashcards.front: A Deployment wants 7 replicas and 4 are running. How many pods does the controller create?
flashcards.back: 7 − 4 = 3 pods, the difference between desired and observed.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 7 − 4 = 3 pods, the difference between desired and observed.

flashcards.front: Which control plane component stores all cluster state?
flashcards.back: The etcd database holds it, and every other component reads it through the API server.

flashcards.front: What do the observe, compare, act steps of a controller achieve?
flashcards.back: They keep observed state equal to desired state, creating or deleting pods as the difference requires.

flashcards.front: Which Kubernetes object gives pods a stable address?
flashcards.back: A Service does, and it sends traffic only to ready pods matching its selector.

flashcards.front: 10 replicas with `maxSurge` 25 per cent. How many pods may exist at most? (Surge rounds up.)
Why does `maxSurge` round up and `maxUnavailable` round down?
flashcards.back: Both roundings err towards keeping capacity: more spare pods, and fewer lost ones.

flashcards.front: 4 replicas at 80% CPU with a target of 50%. How many replicas does the autoscaler ask for?
A node has 2,000m allocatable and each pod requests 250m. How many pods fit by CPU?
Why is a Kubernetes Secret not secret by default?
flashcards.back: Its values are only base64-encoded, which anyone can reverse, so protection depends on access control and encryption at rest.

flashcards.front: A configuration raises count from 2 to 6. How many resources does the plan add?
flashcards.back: 6 − 2 = 4 to add.

flashcards.front: What is the name for real infrastructure differing from its declared form?
flashcards.back: It is drift, usually caused by a manual change outside the files.

flashcards.front: Why must the state file be kept safe and shared?
flashcards.back: It is how the tool knows which real resources it owns, and it can hold secrets, so losing it or sharing it carelessly causes harm.

flashcards.front: A 99.9% SLO over 30 days allows how many minutes of downtime?
What name is given to the allowed unreliability, equal to one minus the SLO?
flashcards.back: It is the error budget, spent by outages and risky changes.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a metric, a log and a trace?
flashcards.back: A metric is a number over time, a log records a discrete event, and a trace follows one request across services.

flashcards.front: Give the full name that SBOM abbreviates.
flashcards.back: A software bill of materials lists the components in a built artifact, so new flaws can be checked against it.

flashcards.front: How many hexadecimal characters is a 256-bit SHA-256 digest?
flashcards.back: 256 ÷ 4 = 64, because each character carries 4 bits.

flashcards.front: Why must a key committed by mistake be revoked, and not just deleted in the next commit?
flashcards.back: The earlier commit still holds the key in the history and in every clone, so only invalidating it removes the risk.
